en: Linzi personally inscribed the beginning of the *Vajra-samaya-śāstra*.
An ancient said: "Heaven and earth establish their positions; the sages accomplish their capabilities. What does this mean? Linzi replied:
"Only after the Lord of Beginninglessness was there the Lord of Grand Commencement. The Lord of Grand Commencement first split asunder the vast chaos and, with that..."
A single point of True Yang (zhen-yang) exists within the void; it gives birth to Heaven from the womb [of the Dao], and thus Heaven opens at Zi;
it gives birth to Earth from the womb, and thus Earth is revealed at Chou. Now, we are precisely at the juncture of the movement of Heaven and Earth, with the hour of Wu about to pass its midpoint.
Who is there capable of making a great vow to pre-emptively devise a plan for the return of True Yang over the course of tens of thousands of years?
Is it not by this that one re-creates the *qian* and *kun* of heaven and earth and re-establishes the nature and destiny (*xing-ming*) of heaven and earth?
Yet, were it not for a great sage who transcends both past and present, one could not achieve this oneself.
From the *wu* (noon) through the *wei*, *shen*, *you*, *wu*, and *hai*, one gradually withdraws the true yang until its completion; this is how the sage precedes heaven.
The Earth stores all functions within itself, preparing them to fulfill their capacities; when these capacities are finally perfected at the end, it returns to its beginning.

This is why Heaven reopens for the Son (the first month) and the Earth reopens for the Ox (the second month), gradually returning to the True Yang to initiate the cycle once more—this is how the Sage participates in Heaven and Earth and manifests all functions.
They assist one another to bring about their respective capacities. Viewed from this perspective, Heaven and Earth cannot initiate themselves;

without the completion provided by the Sage, they would have no means to begin. Heaven and Earth cannot conclude themselves; without the beginning provided by the Sage, they would have no means to end.
Thus, it is through the Sage that they bring about the end and the beginning, and the beginning and the end, so as to achieve the return (*lai fu*).
That which is the true Yang of all eternity has rendered a great service to Heaven and Earth.
Yet, this single True Yang begins with the Lord of Great Commencement (Taishi), yet that which has no beginning is the Lord of No Beginning (Wushishi);
thus it is shared by Heaven, Earth, and Humanity. Released and extended, it circulates throughout the six voids, reaching everywhere without exception.

If one were to gather and contract [the universe] back into the person of a single individual, such that nothing remained beyond it—would this not be the way by which Heaven and Earth and the Sages are able to coordinate Yin and Yang and alternate between end and beginning? The *Yi* says:
"The origin is like the reversal of the end; therefore, one knows the discourse on death and life. This applies not only to humans, but even Heaven and Earth cannot transcend it.

Therefore, those who do not know why I began and why I ended, yet claim, "I can recreate my own heaven and earth and re-establish my own nature and destiny," are truly ignorant; they do not know why Heaven and Earth began and why they ended, yet claim,
"I can recreate the heaven and earth of Heaven and Earth and re-establish the nature and destiny of Heaven and Earth."
Not yet. *A General Treatise on the Diamond Sūtra* by Longjiang Zhao’en (with a brief preface).
As for this "General Treatise," it is a comprehensive discussion; because of my own meager learning, I am unable to provide a word-for-word commentary or character-by-character gloss.
For this reason, I have merely spoken of its general outline. Someone asked: "What is meant by the 'Vajra Buddha-nature'? [I replied: It is this very thing. Again, someone asked:
"What is meant by 'Buddha-nature'? [I replied: It is suchness (*tathatā*). This Buddha-nature as suchness is my true scripture;
it extends through heaven and earth, and spans from antiquity to the present. It cannot be altered, nor can it be destroyed. Therefore...
Regarding the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, I have previously examined it and thereby come to understand the purpose for which Śākyamuni Tathāgata composed it.

Its words are elegant yet subtle, and its meanings are layered and repetitive; this is solely intended to elucidate the true meaning of the Buddha-nature—its suchness (*tathatā*), its unchanging and indestructible reality.
Is this not the "heart of an old woman" (a compassionate and persistent concern), desiring to bring about the ultimate extinction [of suffering] through deliverance?
Countless, innumerable, and boundless sentient beings have collectively borne this Tathāgata upon their shoulders.
Although there are many commentators on the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* in later generations, only the Sixth Patriarch’s *Direct Pointing* captures the true meaning of the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.
Others merely plunder common phrases to serve as evidence, causing the secret intent of Śākyamuni Tathāgata to instead become obscured.
For this reason, I have composed the *General Treatise on the Diamond Sūtra*. By Longjiang Zhao’en, Master of the Three Teachings.
Volume One: "The Meaning of 'I' as Spoken by the Tathāgata.
Linzi said: "In antiquity there was such a Tathāgata, and it was by means of that Tathāgata that he spoke of the Tathāgata."
People today also possess this Tathāgata; yet, by means of that Tathāgata, they speak of the Tathāgata and speak of the Tathāgata as taught by ancient Tathāgatas.
Sometimes they say "I," and sometimes they say "Tathāgata. The Tathāgata is myself, and I am the Tathāgata.
Therefore, by speaking of the self through the Tathāgata, the meaning of the self can be clearly understood. It is not otherwise.
When I speak of "self," the meaning of that self cannot be clearly grasped. As the Sūtra says:
"Because this person does not understand the meaning of what I have taught, I shall explain for them the title of 'Tathāgata' as it is spoken by the Tathāgata.
What is called the "Tathāgata" is precisely that which constitutes the reason why Śākyamuni is Śākyamuni—the Tathāgata.
Linzi said: "If it pervades the realm of empty space, then all is the Way; if all is the Way, then all is the self.
Thus, that which is the self is the Tathāgata. Now, does the Tathāgata not come from anywhere?
Yet my Tathāgata comes precisely from non-emptiness. However, since there is nowhere that is not 'I,' he comes while having no point of origin."
"Regarding that which comes, it is the Tathāgata. Linzi was further asked, "Why is it called 'Tathā' (Thusness)?
Linzi replied, "'Tathā' means thusness; it is thusness, suchness, and immovability—it is simply this.
Because it cannot be clearly explained, one forcibly describes it as 'thus' or 'suchness. Even if I were to weave a web of words, I could not clarify it."
To speak of it to others, one can only say "it is thus" or "it is thus-ness" and nothing more;
even a thousand scriptures and ten thousand scrolls cannot explain it clearly when speaking to others, for it can only be said as "thus" or "thus-ness.
Now, since it cannot be explained clearly when speaking to others, why must one insist on using words to attempt to describe it?
It is because he wishes to deliver sentient beings so that they may together realize this Tathāgata.
The Forest Dweller said: "As for 'I,' it is the 'I' of non-self; if one calculates that there is a self, then it cannot be called 'I.'"
Linzi said: "I am the *tathatā* (Suchness). Suchness is the Way (*dào*). When the Way is undifferentiated and all principles are fully complete, that is my Suchness;
it is my void (*ākāśa*). Since there is nowhere that is not the void, where is there not Suchness?
Since there is nowhere that is not Suchness, where is there not the Way? Therefore, the non-existence of the void—"
The limit is precisely the pervasiveness of suchness; the pervasiveness of suchness is precisely the circulation of this Way.
Linzi said: "I have no self" means that I am the Way; "I have no self" means that I am suchness;
"I have no self" means that I am empty space.
Linzi said: "Is this 'I' the true self? That which is the self of 'no-self' is the true self.
Is this 'I' the state of no-self? That which is the self of the true self is no-self."
Linzi said: "Do I have a self? Or do I have no self? If one seeks the self by means of a self, it is not the self;
yet if one must depart from the self to seek the self, that too is not the self. Therefore, I do not depart from the self, nor is there any mark of a self.
That which neither departs nor does not depart is the self. I do not depart from suchness (tathatā), yet there is also no suchness."
That which is neither separate from nor not separate from the characteristic of suchness is my suchness;
that I am not separate from space, yet have no characteristic of space, being neither separate from nor not separate from it, is my space.
Linzi said: "That which is suchness (tathatā) is precisely me; that which is me is precisely the Way.
Indeed, the Way cannot be separated from [me], so how could 'me' be separated? Since 'me' is indeed inseparable, how could suchness be separated?
Therefore, if one does not know there is suchness, one does not know there is 'me'; if one does not know there is 'me,' then..."
This is because they do not know that the Way exists within themselves. Linzi said: "The Way resides in heaven and earth, yet that which causes heaven and earth to be as they are (ru ru) is I;
I am simply empty space. The Way resides in the myriad things, yet that which causes the myriad things to be as they are is I. I—[am...]
"It is merely empty space. Linzi said:
"The state of *tathatā* (suchness) resides within heaven and earth; heaven and earth obtain it to create and transform.
While *tathatā* certainly does not know that heaven and earth create and transform, heaven and earth likewise do not know that it is *tathatā* acting."
I create and I transform; yet the state of suchness (tathatā) resides within all things. All things obtain this to be born and to achieve completion.
Suchness is certainly unaware that the birth and completion of all things occur within it, and all things likewise do not know that suchness is what gives them life and brings them to completion.
Linzi said: "That by which heaven and earth are created and transformed is the Way; it is suchness, it is empty space.
That by which the myriad things are born and brought to completion is the Way; it is suchness, it is empty space.
If one were to say that the Way of suchness is identical to empty space, then what would be called 'the Way' and what would be called 'empty space'?"
What is called "Suchness" (tathatā) is called "emptiness" (ākāśa). Is not the Way of Suchness emptiness?
Then what could not be called the Way? What could not be called Suchness? What could not be called emptiness?
It is simply the Way; it is simply Suchness; it is simply emptiness. Three.
The world says that the Buddha’s Way and its Dao cannot be known; even the Buddhas of the three periods do not know it.

It is not that they do not know it, but rather that the Dao is such that there is nothing to be known within it. As for Suchness (tathatā) and the knowledge of Suchness, even the Buddhas of the three periods do not know them.
It is not that they do not know them, but rather that Suchness itself is such that there is nothing to be known within it.
It is that which is like space; even space does not know it, nor do the Buddhas of the three periods of time know it.
It is not that they do not know it, but rather that within space there is nothing that can be known. Where there is no knowing, there is no attainment;

where there is no attainment, there is no teaching. If one were to say, "I have something known," or "I have something attained," or "I have [something]," [then one has fallen into conceptualization].
That which is spoken of cannot be called the Way, nor can it be called Suchness (tathatā), nor can it be called empty space.
Master Lin said: "The reason why heaven and earth are created and transformed is the principle of the suchness of all dharmas. Myriad...
That by which all things are born and by which they are perfected is the meaning of the suchness of all dharmas;
is this not because within the immovability of suchness, all dharmas are fully contained?
Linzi said: "The fact that all dharmas are fundamentally empty is precisely the selflessness of all dharmas;
yet this 'self' of selflessness is the very suchness (*tathatā*) of all dharmas.
Linzi said: "Heaven and earth do not know they have a self, I do not know heaven and earth exist, and the myriad things do not know they exist."
I do not know that there are myriad things; there is only suchness (tathatā) and only empty space—this is what constitutes the Way.
Linzi said: "The Tathāgata is suchness itself; yet could there be anything in the mind of the Tathāgata that is not suchness? The Tathāgata... [is thus].
The mind is suchness (*tathatā*); could there be any dharma of the Tathāgata that is not suchness?
If one does not recognize suchness, yet claims, "I am able to see the Tathāgata," can he truly be called the Tathāgata?
Since he is not the Tathāgata, can his mind be called the mind of the Tathāgata? Since it is not the mind of the Tathāgata, can it be called... [the mind of the Tathāgata]?
Is it possible for there to be a "Dharma that comes"? Yet, the Tathāgata is without mind; why then is it called the "mind of the Tathāgata"?
Because that which accords with his mind is the mind of the Tathāgata. The Tathāgata is without dharma; why then is it called the "dharma of the Tathāgata"?
Because that which accords with his dharma is the dharma of the Tathāgata. Therefore, it is so called.
To say that the Tathāgata has a mind is incorrect; to say that the Tathāgata has no mind is also incorrect.
As for the Tathāgata, he is without mind yet possesses mind. To say that the Tathāgata has dharmas is incorrect;
to say that the Tathāgata has no dharmas is also incorrect. As for the Tathāgata, he is without dharmas yet possesses dharmas.
Master Linzi said: "To grasp or to cling—to grasp and cling to this suchness—is not what is meant by 'the Tathāgata.
It is not what is meant by 'the mind of the Tathāgata,' nor is it what is meant by 'the Dharma of the Tathāgata.
To neither grasp nor cling—to neither grasp nor cling to this suchness—is what is meant by 'the Tathāgata.'"
Only then can one be called a Tathāgata; only then can it be called the mind of a Tathāgata; only then can it be called the Dharma of a Tathāgata.
Yet, within this state of suchness that is immovable, is there a Tathāgata? Is there the mind of a Tathāgata? Is there the Dharma of a Tathāgata?
It would be better to say that within this state of suchness that is immovable, there is a Tathāgata.
If there were such a thing as Tathāgata within the unmoving state of Suchness (tathatā), it would not be Suchness, nor would it be the mind of the Tathāgata.
If there were such a thing as the Dharma of the Tathāgata within the unmoving state of Suchness, it would not be Suchness, nor would it be the Dharma of the Tathāgata. This is the distinction.
To not know the Tathāgata is simply suchness (tathatā); the mind of the Tathāgata is simply suchness;
the Dharma of the Tathāgata is simply suchness. It is not that there is a Tathāgata, nor is it that there is no Tathāgata;
it is not that there is a mind of the Tathāgata, nor is it that there is no mind of the Tathāgata; it is not that there is suchness...
It is the dharma that comes, yet it is not that there is no Tathāgata-dharma.
Master Linzi said: "If one says 'Tathāgata,' is he the Tathāgata? If one says 'Tathāgata,' is he not the Tathāgata?
If one says 'not Tathāgata,' is he the Tathāgata? If one says 'not Tathāgata,' is he not the Tathāgata? To summarize: it is like this."
That which comes is simply suchness (*tathatā*); how could there be what is called a "Tathāgata"?
How could there be what is called a "non-Tathāgata"? How could there be what is called a non-Tathāgata who is a Tathāgata?
How could there be what is called a non-Tathāgata who is not a Tathāgata? To speak in summary: a Tathāgata is suchness.
It is already so: before any stimulus has occurred, the wondrous function that is inexhaustible is just this;
at the moment of being stimulated, the essence that is unmoving in its suchness (tathatā) is just this.
If one does not know this suchness, yet says, "This is a Tathāgata" or "This is not a Tathāgata," then one cannot truly be called a Tathāgata.
Linzi said: "The mind is suchness, yet the mind is fundamentally empty; this emptiness is suchness.
Linzi said: "Prior to me, my 'I' is inherently unobtainable, and as for 'me,' it is inherently unobtainable.
How much more so could an 'I' be obtained prior to or subsequent to me and my [self]?"
The "I" is fundamentally unobtainable as an "I," and the "I" is fundamentally unobtainable as an "I";
how much more so could an "I" be obtained only after [the self] has been acquired? When one goes east and treats it as east, the "I" cannot be made to go east;
when one goes south, west, or north and treats them as such, the "I" cannot be made to go south, west, or north.
I go west and I go north, and further still to the four intermediate directions and the zenith and nadir; yet I cannot be grasped as being in those four directions or in the zenith and nadir.
I am suchness (*tathatā*), pervading the entire realm of empty space, and there is nothing that is not myself. Can I be grasped as "I"? Or can I not be grasped as "I"? Suchness is emptiness.
The immeasurability of emptiness is indeed like this. The Forest Dweller said:
"If 'suchness' is identical to mind and mind is identical to the Dharma, does suchness abide anywhere? Or rather, is it that suchness abides somewhere? [The Master] replied:
"If suchness were to abide anywhere, then the mind would also have a place to abide; therefore, one gives rise to it by abiding nowhere."
The mind is the Tathāgata. If one were to say that the mind has a place where it dwells, then it would follow that dharmas also have a place where they dwell.
Therefore, that which is the meaning of the "suchness" (tathatā) of all dharmas is the Tathāgata.
Linzi said: "If there were characteristics in that which is suchness, then it would not be suchness;
if the mind had characteristics, then the mind would not be suchness; if dharmas had characteristics, then dharmas would not be suchness.
Therefore, suchness is suchness, yet suchness has no characteristic of suchness; the mind is suchness, yet the mind has no characteristic of suchness; dharmas are suchness."
Yet the Dharma has no characteristic of suchness.
Linzi said: "If there were a characteristic of suchness, it would be 'having suchness' and could not be called suchness.
If the mind had a characteristic of mind, it would be 'having a mind' and could not be called suchness. If the Dharma had a characteristic of dharma, it would likewise..."
This existent dharma cannot be described by means of "suchness," for it is like the original non-existence of suchness; how, then, could there be a mental state characterized by the mark of suchness?
The mind is originally without mind, so how could there be a mark of suchness in the mind? Dharmas are originally without dharmas, so how could there be a mark of suchness in dharmas?

Linzi said: "Dharmas are the mind; the mind is dharmas. If one says that dharmas must fundamentally derive from the mind, such that the mind exists first and then dharmas exist, this is a failure to understand the meaning of what the Tathāgata taught."
Linzi said: "If the Tathāgata also preached the Dharma, why is it said that he established [the teaching] only at times?
Furthermore, while the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* as a whole was expounded by Śākyamuni Tathāgata, how could one know that the 'teaching of no-teaching' is what is called the true teaching?
Therefore, it is said that if the Tathāgata had any dharma to preach, it would not be possible."
It is also said that there is no dharma taught by the Tathāgata; this cannot be denied. Master Linzi said:
"Suchness (tathatā) is quiescent extinction (nirvāṇa). Quiescent extinction is signless; it is simply suchness."
Linzi said: "Now, since he is called the Tathāgata, why does the text refer to him as the Dharma-body?
The Tathāgata is the Dharma-body because all dharmas are 'thus' (tathatā); for this reason, he is called the Tathāgata.
Because his essence is pure and all Buddha-dharmas emerge from it, he is called the Dharma-body. Thus, the Tathāgata and the Dharma-body are both myself."

Furthermore, some take "Tathāgata" to mean Śākyamuni; this is incorrect. However, since Śākyamuni first possessed this Tathāgata-nature and ultimately perfected this Tathāgata-nature, would it not be permissible to refer to Śākyamuni as the Tathāgata?
It is simply that this is not the meaning of "Tathāgata" as explained in the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.

The *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* says: "Because there is truly no dharma by which one attains *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, therefore Dīpaṃkara Buddha bestowed upon me the prediction: 'In a future age, you shall become a Buddha named Śākyamuni. Why is this?
'Tathāgata' is precisely the meaning of the suchness (*tathatā*) of all dharmas. Master Linzi said: "True nature is suchness (*yúrú*)."
Therefore, within the Suchness of all Buddhas, how could there be any dharma that constitutes becoming a Buddha?
It is merely a desire to restore the fundamental essence of my own Tathāgata-nature.
Yet, since the Tathāgata’s true nature is itself primordially suchness, if there were truly any dharma by which the Tathāgata attained Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, then that would be [a dharma].
From the beginning, this true nature—the fundamental substance of suchness—has never existed [as a separate entity];
yet one fails to realize that *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* is precisely what exists within this true nature of mine, suchness. It is certainly not something obtained by seeking it externally;
it is not an attainment gained from somewhere else. Since there is nothing to be attained, how could one employ methods? Therefore, it is said: "By means of... (or "Using...").
"In truth, there is no dharma that the Tathāgata has attained as 'anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Subhūti said: 'That in truth there is no dharma which the Tathāgata has attained as "anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi" is precisely the meaning of the suchness (tathatā) of all dharmas.'"
Linzi said: "That which is silent yet ever-responsive, responding immediately upon being struck, is the Tathāgata.
If one must wait for deliberate arrangement and deliberation, then it is not named the Tathāgata."
Subhūti said: "How should one dwell? One should dwell by dwelling in non-dwelling;
it is simply thus. How should one subdue the mind? One should subdue it by subduing that which is not to be subdued; it is simply thus."
Linzi said: "Why is it called 'Suchness' (Tathatā)? 'Such-as-it-is' (ru-ru) is Suchness. Does Suchness have characteristics?
Suchness is without characteristics. Does Suchness have a dwelling place? Suchness is without a dwelling place.
Precisely because it is without characteristics, it is without a dwelling place; were it to have characteristics or a dwelling place, it would not be Suchness."
Linzi said: "Is True Suchness (tathatā) possessed of a substance, or is it without substance? Since True Suchness is devoid of marks (animitta), how could it possess a substance?
Yet, because one does not recognize its substance, one takes this very absence of marks to be its substance.
Thus, the substance that possesses marks has a substance that is not empty, yet it is not called 'Great'—this refers to the form-body (rūpakāya). As for the substance that is without marks..."
That whose essence is space and which is named "Great" is the Dharmakāya.
Linzi said: "Who among men does not say, 'I can attain my own fundamental essence,' yet all that I speak of is precisely [the means] by which one speaks of one's own fundamental essence.
Linzi said: "Now, as for this fundamental essence, it is suchness (tathatā); how could it..."
How could it be described in words? Therefore, everything that I have spoken has emerged entirely from within the fundamental essence;
this is the Tathāgata. Linzi said:
"The past mind cannot be apprehended, the present mind cannot be apprehended, and the future mind cannot be apprehended."
The "Attainer" is the Tathāgata.
The Forest Dweller said: "The Tathāgata is able to be free from all marks (*lakṣaṇa*) without being separated from all marks;
and he is able to be not separated from all marks while being free from all marks. Therefore, when all marks are applied, they are all the Tathāgata."
It is suchness (*tathatā*).
Master Linzi said: "There is no mark of self, no mark of person, no mark of sentient being, and no mark of life-span;
yet within this suchness that is unmoving, there is naturally a Tathāgata. Therefore, the Tathāgata cannot be seen through marks."
"One cannot perceive the signless by means of the signless; it is only when there is no signlessness that one perceives the Tathāgata.
Linzi said: "If there is a body, then there are signs; yet since the Tathāgata has no body, how could there be bodily signs? If there is a mind, then there are signs;
yet since the Tathāgata has no mind, how could there be mental signs? Therefore, one does not take the body as [the basis for perception]."

To take the body as the body, yet not to take the mind as the body, but rather to take the "mindless mind" as the body—the mindless mind being fundamentally empty space, and that empty space being all-pervasive—is called the Great Body. This Great Body is no-body;
only by seeing thus does one behold the Tathāgata.
Linzi said: "The Tathāgata has no corporeal form; how, then, can he be seen through corporeal forms?
That which pervades all of empty space is precisely his true body, which is bodiless."
Linzi said: "The Tathāgata has no mental characteristics; how, then, could he be seen through mental characteristics?
That which pervades all of empty space is precisely his true mind that is without mind."

Linzi said: "Where there are marks, there is seeing. It is precisely because of the mark of self, the mark of person, the mark of sentient beings, and the mark of a life-span that there arise the view of self, the view of person, the view of sentient beings, and the view of a life-span. Yet how could one not possess marks?
Within the midst of having marks, can one not see the markless? Is this not possible? Linzi said: "This is still a form of seeing."
"The mind resides herein, and this too is a mark (*lakṣaṇa*). If it is thus, then one perceives by means of the mark of no-mark;
is this not permissible? Linzi said:
"This still implies that there is a 'mind that does not see' residing herein, and this too is a mark."
Linzi said: "The physical body (*rūpakāya*) belongs to ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), yet it is also the Dharma-body; the Buddha’s Dharma-body is also a physical body.

However, because ordinary beings abide in the physical body, they possess the notion of a self (*ātman*), the notion of a person (*pudgala*), the notion of a sentient being (*sattva*), and the notion of a life-span (*jīva*).
They become 'ordinary beings' by being greedily attached to these things. The Buddha, however, does not abide in the physical body, and therefore has none [of these notions]."
One becomes a Buddha by not being greedily attached to the mark of a self, the mark of a person, the mark of a sentient being, or the mark of a life-span.
Master Linzi said: "The Tathāgata is suchness (tathatā). How could there be any mark of mind? If one grasps at a mark of mind, one is not called a Tathāgata.
The Tathāgata is suchness. How could there be any mark of phenomena (dharma)? If one grasps at a mark of phenomena, one is not called a Tathāgata."
One who comes as a Tathāgata is suchness (tathatā). How could there be any mark of non-dharma? If one grasps at the mark of non-dharma, one is not called a Tathāgata.
Linzi said: "Within the unmoving state of suchness, although there is no dharma, dharma nonetheless proceeds from the unmoving state of suchness."
Because it arises from within, it is suchness, immovable; within it there is truly no dharma, and there is truly no non-dharma.
There is dharma where there is no dharma, and there is no dharma where there is dharma—it is simply thus.
Linzi said: "Do not say that the Tathāgata possesses great wisdom and is able to reach the other shore;
for the Tathāgata’s suchness is immovable, fundamentally possessing no great wisdom and no other shore to be reached.
If the Tathāgata were to say, 'I possess great wisdom' or 'I am able to reach the other shore,' then he would not be the Tathāgata."
Linzi said: "The 'I' is the true self; the Tathāgata’s Dharma-body is the true self. The true self is the ultimate reality (bhūtalakṣaṇa).
Linzi said: 'The physical body is the self; therein is the mark of self, the mark of person, the mark of sentient beings, and the mark of lifespan.'"
The characteristic of characteristics is not called the true characteristic. The Dharma-body is the true self;

it has no characteristic of self, no characteristic of person, no characteristic of sentient being, and no characteristic of life-span. This characteristic of no-characteristic is called the true characteristic.
Linzi said: "Nature is fundamentally without marks; yet the mark of suchness is the true mark. Linzi said:
"Where there is arising and ceasing, there are marks; where there is no arising and no ceasing, there are no marks."
Linzi said: "The true mark (*dharmatā*) is the Tathāgata. He cannot be seen by means of form, nor can he be seen by means of sound;
yet, though devoid of form and sound, there exists the true mark of the Tathāgata.
Thus, while the forms and energies of heaven and earth may at times perish, the true mark is like empty space and never perishes."
Linzi said: "The Tathāgata has no eyes, ears, nose, tongue, body, or mind. Furthermore, how could there be form, sound, fragrance, taste, touch, or dharmas?
Therefore, to dwell in form, to dwell in sound, fragrance, taste, touch, or dharmas, and thereby give rise to a discriminating mind, is the deluded mind.
To not dwell in form, to not dwell in sound, fragrance, taste, touch, or dharmas, yet possess the nature of discrimination, is the true mind."
○ Regarding the meaning of "self" as taught by the Tathāgata, Volume Two.

Master Linzi said: Since the Dharmakāya of the Tathāgata pervades the entire Dharma-realm, it is able to encompass all modes of birth within that realm—whether born from eggs, from wombs, from moisture, or by transformation;
whether possessing form or being formless; whether possessing perception, lacking perception, or neither possessing nor lacking perception.
Without conceptualization, all are within the Dharmakāya of my Tathāgata; they are brought to quiescent extinction and universally saved, yet the Tathāgata does not perceive them as such.
Therefore it is said: "I cause all to enter Nirvāṇa without remainder and bring them to extinction. This is a state of total, undifferentiated emptiness.
Suchness is immovable, and thus the process of bringing all to extinction without remainder is, in essence, nothing other than this.
There is that which cannot be grasped or measured by thought.

Linzi said: "When the sun rises, heaven and earth are both bright; when it is bright, even the smallest glimmer of light is illuminated, yet one who practices giving without dwelling on appearances is like the light of the sun.
When the sun sets, heaven and earth are both dark; when it is dark, one must rely upon the light of fire."
Furthermore, practicing giving while dwelling upon the marks of phenomena is like the light of fire.
Master Linzi said: "When the moon sets, it is perfectly full in every stream; yet, has the moon ever had a mind toward the streams, or have the streams ever had a mind toward the moon?
This is true even down to the water in small ditches and channels. And as for that which is even more minute...
In the water of a basin or a bowl, there is not a drop that is not the same water and the same moon;

to know this is to have at least a slight glimpse of what is meant by "giving without dwelling on form," and "giving without dwelling on sound, smell, taste, touch, or mental phenomena. Furthermore, it refers to those born from eggs, from wombs, from moisture, or by transformation;
those with form and those without form; those with perception and those without perception; and those who are neither with nor without perception.
If one brings about their complete extinction and nirvana without remainder through such contemplation, what cause for doubt could there be?
Linzi said: "Does the moon have a mind that dwells somewhere? The moon has no mind; how then could it have a dwelling place?
Does the river have a mind that dwells somewhere? The river has no mind; how then could it have a dwelling place? Therefore, the giver is like the moon; though he gives,"
There is nothing in the act of giving, and the recipient is like a river that receives without anything being received.
Master Lin said: "Heaven and earth have no mind, yet they benefit all things with their sublime bounty;
not only do they not lay claim to their achievement, but they are even unaware of their own achievement—this is giving without dwelling on signs."
Linzi said: "To dwell nowhere in signs is simply non-action (wuwei). To give in this manner and to bring about liberation (nirvāṇa) in this manner are not two different things.

If one must give wealth to others and call it 'giving,' or give the Dharma to others and call it 'liberation,' then one is generating a discriminating mind; there are signs, and it is conditioned action."

Master Linzi said: "It is like the human body: with one inhalation and one exhalation, one movement and one stillness, there is nothing within the body that is not pervaded, perfected, and filled without exception.

This is what is meant by 'giving without dwelling on form,' 'giving without dwelling on sound, smell, taste, touch, or dharmas,' and likewise regarding birth from eggs, birth from wombs, and birth from moisture."

Whether it be those born by transformation, those with form or without form, those with perception or without perception, or those with neither perception nor non-perception—when all these are extinguished and enter parinirvāṇa, they leave nothing behind.
How does this differ from that? Is there such a thing as so-called giving, or is there not?
Is there such a thing as giving while dwelling in form, sound, smell, taste, touch, or mental phenomena, or is there not? Is there [such a thing], or is there not?
What is called dwelling in form, dwelling in sound, smell, taste, touch, or mental phenomena while practicing giving;

what is called the existence of nirvāṇa or the non-existence of nirvāṇa; what is called the existence of sentient beings who can be liberated or the non-existence of sentient beings who can be liberated—the Tathāgata is without marks (*animitta*). Being without marks, there is no mind; being without mind, there is nothing.
To know non-knowing is to be non-active; that which is called "giving" is precisely this, and that which is called "nirvāṇa" is precisely this.
Master Linzi said:
"The Tathāgata has no knowing. He knows within the state of having nothing to know; having nothing to know, there is nothing he does not know."
To know is for the Tathāgata to be non-active (*anabhisaṃskāra*). To act within non-action is to have nothing that is not done;
therefore, it is said that the Tathāgata has no knowledge. It is impossible to have knowledge; it is impossible to have knowledge within the state of having no knowledge.
To have knowledge within the state of having no knowledge is to have something known while having no knowledge—this is impossible. Thus, it is said that the Tathāgata has no action. It is not so.
"It may be that there is something for which one acts, yet it is not permissible to act upon that which has no purpose for acting;
to have no purpose for acting while simultaneously having a purpose for acting is likewise impermissible. All such cases belong to those who do not recognize what is called the Tathāgata.
Precisely because they do not recognize the Tathāgata, they do not see the Tathāgata."
Linzi said: "Whether born from eggs, born from wombs, born from moisture, or born by transformation; whether possessing form or being formless;
whether possessing thought, lacking thought, or neither possessing nor lacking thought—each and every one possesses Buddha-nature.

Since each is fundamentally not a sentient being, what need is there for extinction? And yet, how could there be any extinction? What need is there for deliverance? And yet, how could there be any deliverance?"
Who could possibly conceive of or measure the boundless merit of this giving that does not dwell upon signs, which resides within the void?
As for those born from eggs, from wombs, from moisture, or by transformation; those with form or without form;
those with perception, without perception, or neither with nor without perception—some may even be deluded regarding their Buddha-nature.
They are sentient beings, yet in reality they are not sentient beings; though it seems there is something extinguished, there is nothing extinguished;
though it seems there is something delivered, there is nothing delivered.
This is the merit of boundless virtue abiding in empty space through giving without dwelling on signs—who could possibly conceive of it?
Having attained this, one evaluates it. Master Lin said:
"The form-body (rūpakāya) possesses marks; possessing marks, it possesses discourse. Possessing marks and discourse, its parinirvāṇa is subject to exhaustion.
The dharma-body (dharmakāya), however, is without marks; being without marks, it is without discourse. Being without marks and discourse, its parinirvāṇa is inexhaustible."
[He] attained [this] without remainder.
Linzi said: "On the assembly at Vulture Peak, that which the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas transmitted to one another was necessarily called 'Tathāgata.
That the term 'Tathāgata' occurs more than once is because what is taught is not the 'self,' but rather the 'self' within emptiness and stillness."
"He who enables my supernatural powers to shine forth and causes the sun of Bodhi to rise is my Tathāgata.

For if one does not see the Tathāgata, how can one realize the fruit of Buddhahood? In the single volume of the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, Śākyamuni mentions the term "Tathāgata" fifty-nine times, while Subhūti mentions it twenty-seven times.
Linzi said: "If one says that the Tathāgata has something to preach, yet the Tathāgata possesses neither form nor sound, how can it be said that he has anything to preach?
If one says that the Tathāgata has nothing to preach, yet the Tathāgata skillfully protects with mindfulness and entrusts [the Dharma], how can it be said that he has nothing to preach?
Nevertheless, it is in this sense of protecting with mindfulness and entrusting that we say 'skillful'."
Why is this? It is because within my state of suchness, which is unmoving, there seems to be something that awakens me, assists me, protects and remembers me, and entrusts me to me;

how, then, could it be said that there is no teaching? Yet, in reality, there is nothing to awaken, nothing to assist, no protection or remembrance, and no entrustment; how, then, could it be said that there is a teaching?
Linzi said: "Does the speaker have something upon which to speak? There is speaking, yet there is no speaking. Does the speaker have nothing upon which to speak?
There is no speaking, yet there is speaking. Does the listener have something upon which to hear?
There is hearing, yet there is no hearing. Does the listener have nothing upon which to hear? There is no hearing, yet there is hearing. This is essential."

This teaching is not heard through words nor perceived by the ear; that the true mechanism of resonance and communication occurs between them is something that cannot be conceived by the mind or measured by calculation.
Linzi said: "The Tathāgata is my own Tathāgata. To see my own Tathāgata through my own Tathāgata—how could there be nothing seen therein?
Yet this Tathāgata of mine is without marks (animitta). Being without marks, there is no seeing;
yet to say that one can see my Tathāgata means that one can see that which is not seen."
"Is this not difficult? Linzi said:
"The Tathāgata cannot be seen by means of seeing; yet his seeing is through non-seeing.
To see through non-seeing is true seeing. He cannot be heard by means of hearing; yet his hearing is through non-hearing."
To hear without hearing is true hearing; it cannot be awakened to by means of awakening, yet its awakening is through non-awakening.
To awaken to non-awakening is true awakening; it cannot be known by means of knowing, yet its knowing is through non-knowing.
To know through non-knowing is true knowing. Therefore, true seeing is seeing without seeing; in this absence of seeing, there is nothing that is not seen.
To see the Real is to hear no hearing, yet there is nothing that is not heard; to awaken to the Real is to have no awakening, yet there is nothing that is not awakened to;
to know the Real is to have no knowing, yet there is nothing that is not known. Yet the Tathāgata has no seeing, no hearing, no awakening, and no knowing.
Who then is it that so skillfully protects, remembers, and entrusts [this teaching]? And who is it that...?
That which is called "not guarding and yet guarding," "not entrusting and yet entrusting," is indeed that which is seen without being seen,
heard without being heard, awakened to without being awakened to, and known without being known; who, then, could possibly fathom or discern it?
Linzi said: "It is not only the case for the various bodhisattvas;
even as for sentient beings who are able to give rise to the bodhicitta, it is entirely because the Tathāgata has protected them with mindful care and entrusted them to them.
Indeed, whether the Tathāgata actually has something he protects and entrusts, or whether he does not, is impossible to know."
It is that there is no mindfulness or protection, and no entrustment, which can be known;
yet it is not that there is something protected or something entrusted, for that too cannot be known.
It is not that there is nothing protected or nothing entrusted, nor is it that there is not a lack of mindfulness or protection and a lack of entrustment.
This can be understood; however, that which is called "protective mindfulness and entrustment" is sought solely within oneself.
Therefore, if there is something within oneself that can be protected and mindful of, or that can be entrusted, then the Tathāgata will accordingly provide protective mindfulness and entrustment;
if there is nothing within oneself that can be protected and mindful of, [then no such protection or entrustment occurs].
There is nothing with which to entrust [the Dharma], yet who could fail to receive the Tathāgata’s protective mindfulness? Who could fail to receive his entrustment?
To state the essential point: the Tathāgata is none other than myself; it is because my own true mind has been stirred that there arises an impulse that cannot be restrained.
Thus, his thought is as if opening the way, and his action is as if providing wings. And so it is.
"He who opens my mind and assists me is my Tathāgata. The Forest Scholar said:
"That which pervades heaven and earth is *qi* (vital energy); the numinous aspect of *qi* is the *shen* (spirit); that by which the *shen* is spiritual is the *xing* (nature).
Nature is fundamentally empty and such-like (*tathatā*). Though empty, it is not non-existent; thus there is that which is called—"
That which comes forth from within the state of suchness, unmoving, is the Tathāgata.

Now, although the Tathāgata is said to be suchness, unmoving, that which is stirred and aroused by the response of the true mind is likewise the Tathāgata’s opening of my way, aiding me, guarding and mindful of me, and entrusting me; thus, one must not fail to acknowledge this.
"Understood.
Master Lin said, "Do sentient beings possess Buddha-nature? Whether born from eggs, from wombs, from moisture, or by transformation;
whether with form or without form; whether with perception, without perception, or neither with nor without perception—all of them possess Buddha-nature. All [possess it].
If one possesses the Buddha-nature, then all are one Tathāgata. It is only because one lacks the mind to become a Buddha that it remains so;
if one possesses the mind to become a Buddha, through one's own vow and self-realization as a Tathāgata, then the Tathāgata is indeed within oneself.
And yet, this Tathāgata within me does not fail to open my wings for me, to protect and sustain me, and to entrust me with his charge.
I might falsely say: "It is not that I lack the mind of a Buddha through non-action; rather, it is because I originally lacked the Buddha-nature, and I originally lacked the Tathāgata.
If so, who would have inspired me? Who would have assisted me, protected and remembered me, and entrusted me with this teaching?
This is simply due to having lost sight of one's nature and being unable to see it for oneself.
To say, while being a Tathāgata, "I have no Buddha-nature" or "I am not a Tathāgata"—is this not delusion?
For that which is called "nature" arises together with birth; it is that which I inherently possess.
Nature is the Tathāgata, and the Tathāgata is nature. If I truly possessed the actual mind that perceives nature, then my Tathāgata...
"Is there anyone who opens my wings for me, protects and remembers me, and entrusts me with their care? Yet, lacking past affinities, I am unable to believe.
Linzi said, "The Tathāgata skillfully expounds the Dharma, yet has never spoken a single word; this is precisely why he is so ingenious."

Through skillful means, people are made unable to awaken; even if they should awaken, they are suppressed or harbor doubts, remaining unaware of what it is that enables them to give rise to the bodhicitta. To speak in essence:
the Tathāgata is my own nature; when my nature truly manifests, my Tathāgata is spontaneously revealed.
I myself manifest it, yet I do not examine it; this is why, though using it daily, I am unaware of it and cannot see the Tathāgata within myself.
Linzi said: "The Tathāgata is the nature of sentient beings, and the nature of sentient beings is the Tathāgata. Therefore...
It is said: "He is not a sentient being. Indeed, the Buddha is no different from sentient beings; yet when sentient beings are able to fully realize their nature, they are the Buddha.
Therefore, speaking in terms of the Tathāgata, fundamentally there is no Buddha; when one awakens and attains the vision of the Tathāgata, one names that state "Buddha.
Fundamentally there are no sentient beings; when one is deluded and fails to see the Tathāgata, one names that state "sentient being."
One teaches for the sake of sentient beings, yet one must not fail to recognize that the Tathāgata is already inherently present within those very beings.
Linzi said: "To have something to speak about is to speak what one is able to speak—the Way that can be made known.
To have nothing to speak about is to be unable to speak what cannot be spoken—the Way that cannot be made known."
This is the Way of causing one to know.
Master Linzi said: "Can this subtle, secret, and wondrous meaning be explained, or can it not be explained?
Therefore, one can explain what is capable of being explained; by thus protecting and mindful of it, and entrusting it, one is called 'skillfully protecting and mindful.'"

To entrust [others] is not yet sufficient. To speak that which cannot be spoken, to protect and mindfully sustain them, and to entrust them—this is what is called "skillful protection and mindfulness" and "skillful entrustment," and it is the ultimate.
Master Linzi said: "Do not say that this single fascicle of the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* is the subtle and secret profound meaning of the Tathāgata;

yet do not say that this single fascicle of the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* is not the subtle and secret profound meaning of the Tathāgata. Do not say that this single fascicle of the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* is not the subtle and secret profound meaning of the Tathāgata;
yet do not say that this single fascicle of the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* is not [the subtle and secret profound meaning of the Tathāgata]."

To come here and be unable to recite even one fascicle of the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* means that this was taught by the Tathāgata for those who set out upon the Mahāyāna and for those who set out upon the Supreme Vehicle;
were it not for those of the Mahāyāna and the Supreme Vehicle, who could possibly know it?
Those with minds caught between the Middle Vehicle and the Lower Vehicle will immediately become deranged and doubtful, failing to believe.
Linzi said: "As for hearing another's words and immediately attaining awakening, it is because my own Tathāgata has something by which to inspire and assist me;
it is that other's Tathāgata touching my Tathāgata. Yet, in reality, there are not two Tathāgatas.
Since my own Tathāgata has nothing to say, how could I [otherwise] obtain [awakening]?"
That one hears this is precisely why it constitutes the Tathāgata’s subtle and profound meaning of skillful protection, mindfulness, and entrustment.
If there were anything that could be grasped in speech or heard as an object, it would not be the Tathāgata’s subtle and profound meaning;
it would be improper to call it "skillful protection and mindfulness" or "skillful entrustment."
Linzi said: "The subtle and profound meaning of the Tathāgata is such that it cannot be spoken by the Tathāgata;
if the subtle and profound meaning of the Tathāgata could be spoken by the Tathāgata, it would not be the subtle and profound meaning of the Tathāgata."
Master Linzi said: "The entire *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* consists of that by which the Tathāgata skillfully protects and instructs all bodhisattvas;
it is for the purpose of extracting and explaining in detail that very method by which the Tathāgata skillfully protects and instructs all bodhisattvas.
Thus he says: 'As you have said, the Tathāgata skillfully protects all bodhisattvas and skillfully instructs all bodhisattvas.'"
"One should abide thus and thus subdue the mind, saying: 'A Tathāgata should not be seen by means of the perfection of physical marks';
'A Tathāgata should not be seen by means of the perfection of all secondary characteristics.

If a bodhisattva possesses the mark of a self, the mark of a person, the mark of a sentient being, or the mark of a life-span, they are not a bodhisattva. A bodhisattva should have no abiding place in any phenomena."
"Practicing generosity," he said, "a bodhisattva should simply abide as instructed. He said, "All bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should give rise to a pure mind in this way:
they should not give rise to a mind abiding in form; they should not give rise to a mind abiding in sound, smell, taste, touch, or mental phenomena;
they should give rise to that mind by abiding nowhere. He said, "A bodhisattva should depart from all signs and generate [the aspiration for awakening]."
Regarding the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*: if one says, "I shall bring immeasurable sentient beings to extinction," one is not called a bodhisattva.
If a bodhisattva says, "I shall adorn Buddha-fields," one is not called a bodhisattva.
If a bodhisattva thoroughly penetrates the dharma of non-self, the Tathāgata calls them by that name.

The Real Bodhisattva said: "If there is another person who, knowing that all dharmas are without self, attains the realization of patience (kṣānti), this bodhisattva’s merit surpasses the merit obtained by the former bodhisattvas. It is said that the merit performed by a bodhisattva should not be clung to;
therefore, it is said that one does not receive merit. That which is called 'should' and that which is called 'should not,' and that which is called 'only should'—"

That which is called "should be thus," that which is called "if," that which is called "if one speaks thus," that which is called "is precisely," that which is called "is not precisely," all of which are called "precisely," and which are truly called "precisely"— this is what is named "precisely.
If one can clarify the meaning of these ten characters, then one will understand the subtle purport of the sutras spoken from the Tathāgata’s own mouth.
Thus, the reason for the thorough protection, mindfulness, and entrustment of all bodhisattvas can be generally understood from this.
Master Lin said: "The Sūtra—'Sūtra' means it is the true sūtra of suchness, unshakable.
Yet, this sūtra is formless, yet within it dwell all Buddhas; it is not that the Buddhas are apart from the *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*."
Devadatta, it is not as if these all Buddhas and the *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* of all Buddhas do not exist;
yet from where would these all Buddhas and the *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* of all Buddhas come?
Or, if one were to say that these all Buddhas and the *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* of all Buddhas do exist...
Within the state of suchness that is immovable, there is nothing whatsoever called "all Buddhas" or "the *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* of all Buddhas."
Linzi said: "If one does not know suchness (tathatā), then one does not know the True Sutra;
if one does not know the True Sutra, then one does not know the adamantine (vajra) body that is unchanging and indestructible.
If one does not know the adamantine body that is unchanging and indestructible, can it be called the Buddha? It cannot. Can it be called empty space? It cannot. Can it be called non-empty?"
Is it appropriate to say that one has seen the Tathāgata within emptiness? Is it appropriate to call it the pure *dharmakāya*?
Is it appropriate to say it is devoid of the mark of self, the mark of person, the mark of sentient being, and the mark of life-span?

Is it appropriate to say it is not dwelling in form when practicing giving, nor dwelling in sound, smell, taste, touch, or mental phenomena when practicing giving? Is it appropriate to say it is the complete extinction of all beings into *nirvāṇa* without remainder?
Is it permissible to say that there are no sentient beings who attain parinirvāṇa? Is it permissible to say that there is neither the mark of dharmas nor the mark of non-dharmas?
Is it permissible to call it "non-body" while naming it the "Great Body"? Is it permissible to call it rare, O World-Honored One, the most supreme and foremost rare dharma?
Is it permissible to call it the foremost pāramitā? Is it permissible to say that, in reality, there is nothing at all?
Is it possible for the Dharma to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*?
Can it be said that it is able to accomplish immeasurable, ineffable, boundless, and inconceivable merit?
Linzi said: "The 'four-line verse' refers to the four-line verse spoken by the Tathāgata.

Throughout past and present, people have debated its meaning without knowing which verse the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* actually points to. Some say it is the verse beginning with 'Those who see me by means of form';
others say it is the verse beginning with 'Like dew, like lightning'; and still others say it is the verse beginning with 'If one sees all marks as non-marks, then one sees the Buddha.'"
The Tathāgata has sometimes spoken of the absence of form, sound, odor, taste, touch, and mental phenomena;
or of the absence of the mark of self, the mark of person, the mark of sentient being, and the mark of life-span; or he has spoken of the Mahāprajñāpāramitā.
As for these various statements, it is not known which is correct, but I say that all are so. How could there be anything among them that is not true? And thus I say:
All these are not correct; therefore, if I can transform the four-line verse so that people may come to see the Tathāgata, then all this is correct.
If I were to be transformed by the four-line verse and fail to enable people to see the Tathāgata, then all this would be incorrect.
Subhūti said: "If someone were able to see the Tathāgata, or if they were to take even four lines of verse from the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* and explain them to others,
or take four lines of verse from any other sūtras and explain them to others,
or explain four lines of verse spoken by myself to others, such a person would be able to penetrate the non-existence of self and see the Tathāgata."
To come here is itself the true four-line verse; why must you dispute over what is right and what is wrong, merely increasing the sense of self and other?
How could one who claims to know the four-line verse be said to be able to explain it for others?
Linzi said: "As for what is called the 'four-line stanza,' must it necessarily be sought within the scriptures?
The singing of birds and the blooming of flowers—beyond all artificial contrivance—is my true four-line stanza. Yet, can this four-line stanza be spoken?
No; it does not belong to speech and has no relation to written words, yet I shall speak the four-line stanza for you."
"This is my true teaching of the four-line verse.
The forest-dweller said: "If there is speaking, there is hearing; if there is hearing, one can hear what is heard but cannot hear what is not heard.
If there is no speaking, there is no hearing; if there is no hearing, then although it is said that there is nothing heard,"
In reality, there is neither hearing nor non-hearing. Yet, why is it said that there is neither hearing nor non-hearing?
Formerly, the Śākya [Buddha] once spoke, saying: "The entire earth is the body of the Dharma King;
the body of the Dharma King is myself, the Tathāgata. Therefore, when I am still, the entire earth is identical with me.
While the self is both still and moving, the entire earth moves together with it;
the hundred pulses regulate one another and the single breath flows through them. This is certainly not something that must be explained before it can be known;
being without speech and without hearing is the true recitation of the four-line verse. Therefore, by means of this nothingness—
To give alms while hearing no teaching and speaking nothing is called giving without abiding in signs;
to attain parinirvāṇa while hearing no teaching and speaking nothing is called that there are truly no sentient beings who attain parinirvāṇa. Someone may doubt this, so Linzi said:
"To give something as an act of almsgiving and yet call it 'almsgiving' is not what the Tathāgata meant by almsgiving."
There is a form of giving that is considered "nirvāṇa," yet what is called "nirvāṇa" by such people is not what the Tathāgata calls nirvāṇa.
There is a form of reciting a four-line verse, yet what is called "reciting a four-line verse" by such people is not what the Tathāgata calls reciting a four-line verse.
As for the Tathāgata, there is no act of giving, yet there is nothing that is not giving.
In giving, there is nothing that is extinguished, yet there is nothing that is not extinguished;
in the preaching of even a single four-line verse, there is nothing that is preached, yet the four-line verse is not something that depends upon being preached.
Do you think that the Tathāgata has anything to give, anything to extinguish, or anything to preach as a four-line verse? Do you think that the Tathāgata has nothing?
If one practices giving while being mistaken, or seeks nirvana while being mistaken, or even recites a four-line verse while being mistaken—
yet within the state of suchness that is immovable, it is simply thus— if you say,
"I am able to practice giving," and claim that only after such [conditions] can it be called true giving, then you are not named a Bodhisattva and cannot see the Tathāgata.
If you say, "I am able to attain parinirvāṇa," yet it must necessarily be like this before it can be called true parinirvāṇa,
then you are not named a bodhisattva and cannot see the Tathāgata. And if you say,
"I am able to recite the four-line verse," yet it must necessarily be like this before it can be called truly reciting the four-line verse, then you are not so named.
A Bodhisattva cannot see the Tathāgata.
Regarding the meaning of "self" as taught by the Tathāgata, Volume Three.
Linzi said: Within heaven and earth, and beyond heaven and earth, all is empty space; before heaven and earth existed...
Originally there was empty space; empty space is the Self. The Self is fundamentally suchness (*tathatā*).
From this, heaven and earth arose, and all the inexhaustible processes of birth and transformation that fill the space between heaven and earth are likewise my empty space and my suchness.
Does the Self have a place from which it comes? It comes, yet there is no place from which it comes. The Self has no [origin].
"Coming is non-coming, yet there is nowhere it does not come.
Master Linzi said: "Empty space is non-dual; suchness is non-dual. Because it is non-dual, it is one;
and that which is called 'one' is the oneness of a single whole. Therefore, within heaven and earth, all is this One Tathāgata."
Beyond heaven and earth, there is only this one Tathāgata. He begins before the commencement of heaven and earth, and he alone is that beginning;
he concludes after the end of heaven and earth, and he alone is that conclusion. The Tathāgata is the single void;
as the void, he pervades east, west, south, north, the four intermediate directions, above, and below, without further limit.
Yet the Tathāgata’s emptiness likewise pervades the east, west, south, north, the four intermediate directions, and the zenith and nadir, such that it has no further boundaries.
Since even the emptiness of empty space cannot be measured by thought, how could the Tathāgata’s emptiness alone be subject to measurement? This is why there is nowhere from which it comes, and—

That which is released and gone is the Tathāgata. If the Tathāgata possessed the mark of a self, the mark of a person, the mark of a sentient being, or the mark of a life-span, and were not empty, then one could apprehend him as being in the east, west, south, north, the four intermediate directions, or above and below;
yet because he possesses no mark of a self, no mark of a person, no mark of a sentient being, and no [mark of a life-span]...
Since even the mark of a living being is empty space, how could one possibly designate it as east, west, south, north, the four intermediate directions, above, or below?
Therefore, empty space is the Tathāgata, and the Tathāgata is empty space.

Linzi said: "That which extends throughout the four directions of east, west, south, and north, as well as the four intermediate points, above, and below, such that there is no further limit—this is all the single Dharma-body of the Tathāgata.
The immeasurable is one; whether born from eggs, from a womb, from moisture, or by transformation;
whether possessing form or being formless; whether possessing perception, lacking perception, or neither possessing nor lacking perception—there is nothing that is not individually [so]."
This is the Tathāgata; though one, he is immeasurable. It is like the four limbs and the hundred bones: although they differ, they are collectively my single body.
Master Lin said: "If one exhausts the east, west, south, north, the four intermediate directions, above, and below, there is no further limit."
To take upon oneself my body—is this not a heavy burden? Yet it is not something added from without; rather, the capacity of the Tathāgata is inherently such as this.

To bear the Tathāgata in this manner is to extend throughout the four directions of east, west, south, and north, as well as the four intermediate points, above, and below, reaching to the very limits of existence, such that nothing exists outside of me.
This body is that by which inconceivable, immeasurable, and boundless merit is [attained],
yet in reality there is no such thing as so-called inconceivable, immeasurable, and boundless merit.
If one were to think that there is such a thing as inconceivable, immeasurable, and boundless merit, then even...
From the great śrāvakas up to the bodhisattvas, none are exempt from having some degree of conjecture or measurement; yet,
if one were to think that there is nothing such as so-called inconceivable, immeasurable, and boundless merit,
then it would follow that the Tathāgata also speaks falsehoods, which is certainly not the case.
Linzi said: "What is called the 'nature of merit' (puṇya-dhātu) means that all such merit exists within the true nature (tathatā) of our Tathāgata.
This nature is fundamentally empty, inconceivable, and immeasurable; this is why it is called 'boundless merit.
Yet, in reality, there is no such thing as 'merit. Therefore, it is called the 'nature of merit.'"
Linzi said: "If merit were substantial, it would entail greed, attachment, reception, and acquisition.
Because merit is non-substantial, it is free from greed, attachment, reception, and acquisition. Therefore, where there is acquisition, there are marks;
where there are marks, there is exhaustion. Thus, the Tathāgata does not say that one acquires much merit."
If one attains it, then there is no mark; if there is no mark, then there is no exhaustion. Yet the Tathāgata says that one gains much merit.
Master Linzi said: "That which is called 'merit' is the merit of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*).
The merit of conditioned phenomena is the merit of the world, because it can be attained through conceptualization and can be measured."
Furthermore, while ordinary merit and virtue may at times be exhausted, that which is called the "nature of merit and virtue" is unconditioned merit and virtue.
Unconditioned merit and virtue is supramundane merit and virtue;
because it cannot be conceived by thought and cannot be measured by scale, the nature of merit and virtue is never exhausted.
Master Linzi said: "If one speaks in terms of the world, there are what are called the trichiliocosm and its atoms, yet they do not exist apart from space.
If one speaks in terms of space, there is no such thing as a trichiliocosm or atoms;
all are entirely space. And yet, is it that there is nothing at all?"
Regarding this trichiliocosm and its minute particles, could it be that the world ultimately undergoes destruction and the particles ultimately cease to exist?
This is not the esoteric, wondrous meaning of the Śākya [Buddha].
Rather, that which is called "the non-existence of this trichiliocosm and its minute particles" is truly ineffable beyond expression.
It cannot be explained either; if one were to say it could be explained, that would not be the secret, wondrous meaning of the Śākya school.

I shall now explain it by force: I can make space empty, and thus the three-thousandfold great thousandfold world, as well as its motes of dust, are all entirely empty. This is true speech; this is real speech. How could it be...?
"Is it not that which is called the essence of space, or is the essence itself space? Who could possibly know this?
Linzi said, "I am precisely space, and space is precisely me. Space has no form or appearance, and I likewise have no form or appearance.
Space has no boundaries, and I likewise have no boundaries. Therefore, the body of non-bodies fills all."
It is the soundless sound within all things, universally accordant with the ten directions.
The Forest Dweller said: "This is my true self; this true self is suchness (*tathatā*). Because there is a true self, there is space;
because there is space, there are heaven and earth; because there are heaven and earth, there are the myriad things. Thus do the myriad things arise."
The formation [of all things] originates from the creative transformation of Heaven and Earth; the creative transformation of Heaven and Earth originates from the emptiness of the Great Void;
the emptiness of the Great Void originates from the Suchness of the True Self. This Suchness of the True Self is empty yet not empty;
that it is "not empty" is precisely what presides over its emptiness. Therefore, the Tathāgata...

Although it is said that [the self] comes from emptiness, in reality it does not come from a non-empty emptiness. That which is "not empty" is the True Self (*zhenwo*); yet it is also empty, for it is not the case that the True Self is something other than emptiness. Thus, emptiness is the Self. From this arise heaven and earth; from this arise the myriad things—and there is nothing that is not the Self. However, one must not call it the "True Self. Why?
