I am non-self, yet the true emptiness is not empty. Precisely because it is not empty, it is able to give rise to space;
because space is boundless, it is able to give rise to heaven and earth; because heaven and earth are vast and great, they are able to give rise to the myriad things.
That space, being boundless, can give rise to heaven and earth, and that heaven and earth, being vast and great, can give rise to the myriad things—this is so.
All these are instances of that which is both empty and not-empty having something to preside over them;

as for what is called "giving without dwelling on signs," who indeed could fathom or recognize it? Whether born from eggs, from wombs, from moisture, or by transformation; whether possessing form or being formless;
whether possessing perception, lacking perception, or neither possessing nor lacking perception—all such beings are encompassed within my vast heaven and earth.
Within the vastness of the great void, which is boundless, I thereby came to know that the sun, moon, stars, and constellations do not possess me;
yet the sun, moon, stars, and constellations have no means by which to illuminate or preside over me. The thunder, lightning, wind, and rain do not possess me;
yet the thunder, lightning, wind, and rain have no means by which to stir or moisten me. As for the mountains, peaks, rivers, and seas—
Were it not for the existence of the "I," the mountains, rivers, and seas would have no means to flow or stand firm;
were it not for the existence of the "I" within insects, plants, and trees, insects, plants, and trees would have no means to grow or sustain themselves.
Thus, although that which makes the myriad things what they are may be said to be rooted in Heaven and Earth, it is the "I" that upholds the myriad things.
That which is called "things" is also heaven and earth, and it is also myself.

Although that by which heaven and earth constitute heaven and earth is said to be fundamentally based upon empty space, that which maintains and upholds heaven and earth is also empty space, and it is also myself.
Therefore, as for what is called "giving without abiding in signs," who indeed could [attain it]?
He measured and discerned this.
Master Lin said: "That which causes the myriad things to be the myriad things is because they possess the 'I.

It is through the 'I' that one takes the 'I' as the 'I,' and it is the 'I' that causes the myriad things to be generated and sustained. It is the 'I' that causes Heaven and Earth to be Heaven and Earth."
This is because there is a "self" within them; it is the self that creates itself, and thus the self is that which brings about the transformations of heaven and earth.
It is because there is a "self" within it that space is what it is as space;
it is the self that creates itself, and thus the self is that which constitutes space as space.
Linzi said: "The Way of Heaven is lofty and luminous; were it not for my emptiness and my suchness, there would be nothing by which it could be lofty or luminous. The Way of Earth is vast and thick;
were it not for my emptiness and my suchness, there would be nothing by which it could be vast or thick. It began before the beginning of heaven and earth."
If there were not this emptiness of my self and this suchness of my self, then although heaven and earth are vast, they would have no means to initiate their beginning;
and after the end of heaven and earth, they would have no means to conclude their ending. Viewed from this perspective, as for heaven and earth—
Height, clarity, breadth, thickness, beginning, and end—all depend upon my emptiness and my suchness;
being thus, who could possibly fathom or discern them?
Linzi said: "At first, one transforms through spirit and vital energy (shenqi), yet one still knows there is nature and destiny (xingming).
Later, one transforms through nature and destiny, yet one still knows there is empty space (xukong). However, that which is birthless is empty space;
how could it be said that one simply does not know there is nature and destiny? One also does not know there is empty space."
Therefore, when there is neither non-emptiness nor non-non-emptiness, neither non-vacuity nor non-non-vacuity, and neither non-arising nor non-non-arising,
only then can it be called the perfect, pure, and remainderless *nirvāṇa*,
the supreme vehicle (*ekayāna*) and ultimate ground of the Śākya clan.

Linzi said: "If there is neither non-emptiness nor that which is not non-empty, and neither non-vacuity nor that which is not non-vacuous, then destiny is established by oneself and nature emerges from oneself;
even Heaven and Earth cannot then define one's nature or decree one's destiny.
Since destiny is established by oneself and nature emerges from oneself, it is divine without being a spirit and is vital energy without being mere qi."

Yet Heaven and Earth cannot even divine me or constitute my vital energy (*qi*); how could it be said that Heaven and Earth fail to divine me, constitute my *qi*, my nature (*xing*), or my destiny (*ming*)?
This is not all. I shall employ my spirit and vital energy to divine and constitute the spirit and vital energy of Heaven and Earth, and the spirit and vital energy of the myriad things;
for there are Heaven, Earth, and the myriad things that do not rely upon my spirit for their existence.

Do the spirits rely on my vital energy (*qi*) to constitute their own energy? Or do I, through my nature and destiny (*xing-ming*), cause heaven and earth and all things to constitute their own nature and destiny?
Yet, do heaven, earth, and all things not rely on my nature to constitute their own nature, and rely on my destiny to constitute their own destiny?
This is the practice of giving without dwelling upon signs, and it is further situated in this.
The spirit, energy, nature, and destiny are just like this; who could possibly fathom or discern them?
Master Lin said: "Why is it called 'the Tathāgata’s skillful means (upāya) for penetrating deeply into the nature of sentient beings,' and why is the nature of sentient beings the Tathāgata?
This is what makes his skillful means so excellent—it is not that there is some fixed direction or method."
"Exactly so," said Linzi.
"The Tathāgata is one who acts through non-action and yet there is nothing he does not do.

Precisely because he acts through non-action and yet there is nothing he does not do, he is able to penetrate deeply into the nature of all things to preside over them and provide skillful means for them."
Do not say that the Tathāgata is able to penetrate deeply into the nature of the myriad things to sustain and skillfully guide them;
rather, it is because he is able to penetrate deeply into the nature of Heaven and Earth to sustain and skillfully guide Heaven and Earth.
You must not say that the Tathāgata is able to penetrate deeply into the nature of Heaven and Earth to sustain and skillfully guide Heaven and Earth.
Furthermore, he is able to penetrate deeply into the nature of space to take space as his locus through skillful means;
in the true practice of giving, nothing surpasses this. Not only does he not dwell in signs, but there is not even a sign in which he can dwell.
Subtler than the subtle—who could possibly fathom or discern him?
Linzi said: "If one cannot forget life, one cannot attain the Unsurpassed; if one cannot be free from birth, one cannot become a Buddha.
Therefore, those who take the nature and life of their parents as their own nature and life still know that there is a body;
and because they still know there is a body, they cannot forget life. They do not, by means of the nature and life of their parents, create their own nature."
One who has realized the nature of life is one who does not perceive a body; because they do not perceive a body, they are able to realize non-arising.
Therefore, it is only when one can remain free from anger even while having their limbs severed joint by joint that they may truly be said to have forgotten birth and attained non-arising.
Linzi said: "In the suchness of empty space, how could there be a trichiliocosm? How could there be even a single mote of dust?
In the suchness of empty space, one sees neither heaven above nor earth below, nor does one see the boundaries of the east, west, south, north, or the four intermediate directions;
how much less, then, can there be within heaven and earth what are called 'worlds' or 'motes of dust'?"
Linzi said: "The three thousandfold world-system exists entirely within the void of my Dharma-body;
it is not the world-system itself, yet that which takes the world-system as its mind is the world-system.

The three thousandfold world-system, though ground into fine dust, exists entirely within the void of my Dharma-body; it is not the fine dust itself, yet that which takes the fine dust as its mind is the fine dust."
Linzi said: "If there is a mind that departs from the world, it is because one is obstructed by the world and thus intentionally leaves it;

can this be called a 'mind without a world'? If there is a mind that departs from atoms, it is because one is obstructed by atoms and thus intentionally leaves them; can this be called a 'mind without atoms'?"
Master Linzi said: "Where there is mind, there is form; where there is form, there is a world; where there is a world, there are atoms.
Where there is no mind, there is no form; where there is no form, there is no world; where there is no world, there are no atoms.
Therefore, the moment a single thought arises, it is already form, it is already a world, and it is already atoms—a hair’s breadth of attachment."
"To say 'it has marks' is itself the world and itself the motes of dust.
Linzi said, "Do not tell me that Prajñāpāramitā is not Prajñāpāramitā;
do not tell me that what is not Prajñāpāramitā is Prajñāpāramitā. By what standard do you determine what is correct?"
By what means is your prajñāpāramitā yours? That which is not yours is your prajñāpāramitā.
If your mind dwells upon the prajñāpāramitā, it possesses marks;
it is a world and it is like motes of dust—it would then not be prajñāpāramitā. If your mind...
To abide in what is not the prajñāpāramitā is also to possess signs, and it is also the world and also atoms; thus, it is not the prajñāpāramitā.
Master Linzi said: "There is a world of dharmic characteristics, which is a mote of dust; there is a world of non-dharmic characteristics, which is a mote of dust;
there is a world of neither-dharmic-nor-non-dharmic characteristics, which is a mote of dust. There is a world of subject and object, which is a mote of dust;
there is a world of neither-subject-nor-object, yet possessing the characteristics of neither-subject-nor-object, which is a mote of dust."
Even a single mote of dust is without subject or object, yet it possesses the characteristic of being without subject or object; such is the world, even down to a single mote of dust.
Master Linzi said: "To have that which can create the Buddha-mind is a world, even down to a single mote of dust; to lack that which can create the Buddha-mind..."
There are worlds as numerous as atoms where there is no mind that can become a Buddha; there are worlds as numerous as atoms where there is a mind that can deliver sentient beings;
and there are worlds as numerous as atoms where, though there is no mind that can deliver sentient beings, one gives rise to the mind that can deliver sentient beings.
Linzi said: "To claim that one has attained anything regarding unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment, while still maintaining the mind that 'attains,' is the world;

it is a mote of dust. To claim that one has not attained anything regarding unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment, while still maintaining the mind that 'does not attain,' is the world; it is a mote of dust."
Linzi said: "To say, 'I am able to possess great wisdom and reach the other shore,' yet still maintain a mind that seeks realization—this is the world;

this is a mote of dust. Is it not also the case that to say, 'I do not maintain a mind that seeks realization,' yet still maintain a mind that dwells upon non-realization—this too is the world; this too is a mote of dust?"
Linzi said: "If one perceives the world with a defiled mind, the world is a single speck of defilement;
if one perceives the world with a pure mind, the world is a single purity;
if one perceives the world with a mind of emptiness, the world is a single emptiness. Yet, there is still that which is called 'emptiness' itself."
This means that while space exists and there are so-called worlds, one must reach a point where one does not know the existence of worlds nor the existence of space;
where space encompasses the world yet one does not know the space of the world,
and the world encompasses space yet one does not know the world of space— only then can it be called "emptiness."

That which is empty and void is suchness (*tathatā*). Is this not the Tathāgata within myself—the one who creates the spirit and vital energy, who creates nature and destiny, and who renders them empty and makes them suchness?
Linzi said: "O Lady, who does not possess true nature? Who does not possess a true self? Who does not possess the Tathāgata?
To see the Tathāgata for oneself is to see one's own true nature; to see one's own true nature is to see one's own true self.
Furthermore, Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi likewise arises from within the unmoving state of suchness."
Because you have personally awakened and awakened others, being pure and perfect, you are called a Buddha.
Master Lin said: "If you do not recognize the Tathāgata, you do not recognize me; since you do not recognize me, how can you become a Buddha?"
Linzi said: "The 'self' of the Tathāgata can universally manifest throughout all things, yet the 'self' of sentient beings is fully present within the Tathāgata.
If sentient beings do not accord with the Tathāgata, it is not because the Tathāgata lacks self;
rather, it is because the Tathāgata is free from self while sentient beings are deluded by their possession of a self."
He came forward.
Master Linzi said, "Sentient beings are fully endowed with the Tathāgata, yet the Tathāgata says they are not sentient beings.
If sentient beings were able to see the Tathāgata, they would be without the mark of self, the mark of person, the mark of sentient being, and the mark of life-span."

Sentient beings are precisely those who possess the notion of a self, the notion of a person, the notion of a sentient being, and the notion of a life-span, and thus are unable to see the Tathāgata; such are sentient beings.
Master Lin said: "Pervading the realm of empty space, there is not a single thing that is not within the Tathāgatagarbha; there is not a single thing that is not [the Tathāgata]."
Within this Tathāgatagarbha, there is not a single thing that is not Buddha;
yet, while sentient beings’ own selves already fully possess the Tathāgata and pervade the realm of empty space, why is it that so few are able to become Buddhas? What is the reason for this?
Linzi said: "I have no Buddha; if one deludes me, I become a sentient being. I have no sentient beings;
if one awakens to me, I become a Buddha."
Linzhi said: "The Buddha is one with me; I am the Buddha. Since I am the Buddha, how could there be a Buddha to be made?
Sentient beings are also one with me; I am sentient beings. Since they are not [separate from] sentient beings, how could there be sentient beings to be saved?"
Master Linzi said: "The true nature is the original nature.
Now, what is called the original nature is it not that which existed of its own accord as my very essence prior to birth? Therefore, the true nature is the true self."
Linzi said: "Generally speaking, when one speaks of 'I,' it is the true self. To say 'there is an I' while identifying it with the physical form of the body is not the self.
Is it not the case that the physical form exists? If one identifies the self with nature and destiny (xing-ming), that is not the self.
Is it not the case that nature and destiny exist? If one identifies the self with empty space, that is not the self. Therefore, there is a self."
If there is the mark of a self, the mark of a person, the mark of a sentient being, the mark of a life-span, or any marks at all, then "I" am a self,
and yet it is not a self; if there is no self, then there is no mark of a self,
no mark of a person, no mark of a sentient being, and no mark of a life-span, and thus there are no marks at all— this "I" is the true self.
Linzi said: "Now, in becoming a Buddha, how could there be no Dharma? Yet that which the world calls 'Buddha-dharma' is not the true Buddha-dharma.
Thus, at first one uses spirit and breath to create transformation for oneself and returns to one's nature and life;
later, one uses nature and life to create transformation for oneself to realize non-arising. Such a Buddha-dharma is what I call it."
Those who take the Daoist teachings as their entry point are precisely such people;
having realized non-arising and furthermore forgotten all dharmas, is this not what is called the most supreme, foremost, and rare Buddha-dharma?

Yet, it is only by means of this most supreme, foremost, and rare Buddha-dharma that one may realize this unsurpassed, profoundly deep, and subtle fruit of Buddhahood, after which one may finally [attain it].
One may speak of suchness; one may speak of empty space; one may speak of the True Sutra; one may speak of the adamantine body that is immutable and indestructible;
one may speak of the absence of the mark of self, the mark of person, the mark of sentient being, and the mark of life-span;
one may speak of not abiding in form when practicing giving, and not abiding in sound, fragrance, taste, touch, or dharmas when practicing giving; and one may speak of total extinction.

Having delivered them without exception, yet there is truly no sentient being who has attained deliverance; only then can one speak of the absence of the mark of dharmas and the absence of the mark of non-dharmas;
only then can one speak of the non-body and the great body; only then can one speak of the foremost *pāramitā*;
only then can one speak of the fact that there is truly no dharma by which one attains *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*; only then can one speak of accomplishment.
With immeasurable, ineffable, boundless, and inconceivable merit, one may then speak of the Tathāgata as "rare," O World-Honored One.
It is by virtue of this that what is called the Pure Dharmakāya is Vairocana Buddha; the Perfect Reward Body (Saṃbhogakāya) is Rocana Buddha;
and the hundreds of thousands of millions of Transformation Bodies (Nirmāṇakāya) are Śākyamuni Buddha. This is how they are distinguished.
○ Regarding the meaning of the "Self" as taught by the Tathāgata, Volume Four.
Master Linzi said: "One relies on the creative transformation of one's parents to create one's physical body (*rūpakāya*);
yet the Tathāgata of the physical body is not my true Tathāgata. One establishes the creative transformation of one's own person to create my Dharma-body."
The Tathāgata who is the Dharma-body is indeed my own Tathāgata.
While it is certainly said that the Tathāgata of the Dharma-body is the very essence of empty space, can the Tathāgata of the form-body (rūpakāya) likewise be called the essence of empty space?
Linzi said: "Do not say that this trichiliocosm is what is called a 'trichiliocosm.
That which is called a 'trichiliocosm' is not this so-called trichiliocosm. Do not say that these atoms of this trichiliocosm are [atoms]..."
It is the atom of a thousand great trichiliocosms; yet that which is called the atom of a thousand great trichiliocosms is not this very atom of a thousand great trichiliocosms.
Worlds are inexhaustible, and each individual world contains its own thousand great trichiliocosms and three thousand [great chiliocosms].

The atoms within a thousandfold world-system are likewise inexhaustible; though these atoms are inexhaustible, each individual atom contains a trichiliocosm and the atoms of that trichiliocosm, all of which are also inexhaustible.
This is like mirrors reflecting one another until they penetrate each other completely, or like pearls illuminating one another; such is their perfect interfusion.
It is said: "That which is not a unified aggregate is called a unified aggregate. It is further said:
"A unified aggregate is that which is ineffable. Master Linzi said: "The Tathāgata of the Dharma-body pervades all of space; yet within the trichiliocosm..."
The realm that exists within the Tathāgata’s empty space is but a single bubble in the great ocean.

As for the Tathāgata as a physical body (rūpakāya), can he truly be considered the Tathāgata? Therefore, there are times when one attains awakening and, though designated by the name "Buddha," suddenly falls into delusion once more—such a person is still a sentient being.

Linzi said: "The immeasurable, innumerable, and boundless sentient beings who were all encompassed within my own life-force and extinguished by the void—this is what is meant by 'extinguishing and delivering immeasurable, innumerable, and boundless sentient beings.
It does not mean that immeasurable, innumerable, and boundless sentient beings can extinguish themselves and deliver themselves to become Buddhas."

Master Linzi said: "All sentient beings originally possess this very nature and life; what is called 'creating one's own nature and life' is simply the restoration of that which one inherently possesses.
By means of this, one empties [the mind], and that which is thus revealed is the so-called 'original countenance.
How could the original countenance be called 'sentient beings'? It is only because of delusion that it is so designated."
That which the parents call "nature and destiny" (xingming) as nature and destiny refers to sentient beings.
Master Lin said: "The Tathāgata speaks of the foremost *pāramitā*, yet it is not a foremost *pāramitā*.
Only one who can personally effect transformation and remain in emptiness can attain this foremost *pāramitā*."
To summarize the essential point: that which is called the foremost pāramitā is indeed not something to be attained, nor is it something to be attained within the realm of form and characteristics.
Master Linzi said: "One creates one's own nature and life, yet within that void there naturally exists a true mark (*dharmatā*).
Therefore it is said: 'This is precisely the non-mark. For this reason, the Tathāgata spoke of it by the name 'true mark.
The true mark is the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*). Only after [realizing] this true mark of the void—that is, the true mark of the Dharma-body—does one [attain it]."
"He may be called the Tathāgata.
The forest-dweller asked, "Can one see the Tathāgata by means of physical marks? Yet the Tathāgata has no physical marks.
Rather, the physical marks of the Tathāgata are themselves the work of transformation; that which perceives these physical marks is not itself a physical mark. Therefore it is said:"
The physical marks described by the Tathāgata are, in fact, not physical marks.
The Forest Dweller said: "Since the Dharma-body Tathāgata possesses no eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind, how could there be any form upon which he might dwell and give rise to a thought?
Furthermore, how could there be any sound, odor, taste, touch, or mental object upon which he might dwell and give rise to a thought?"
Linzi said: "A Bodhisattva should give rise to the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* while remaining detached from all marks (*nimitta*).
If one does not know that one is the creator of oneself and that [the self] is like empty space, this is precisely being unable to detach from this physical body.
Being unable to detach from this physical body is precisely being unable to be without the mark of self (*ātman*), the mark of person (*pudgala*), and the mark of sentient beings (*sattva*)."
If one who lacks the mark of a life-span cannot be without the mark of a self, the mark of a person, the mark of a sentient being, or the mark of a life-span,
yet claims to be able to give rise to the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, I do not know such a person.
Linzi said: "The *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* attained by the Tathāgata is that which is self-transformed and realized within emptiness;
it is this *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, and not the *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* as it is commonly understood in the world."
Subhūti said: "Does the Tathāgata have anything attained that is called *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*? Does the Tathāgata have any dharma taught? The Tathāgata is like space;
he has nothing attained regarding *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, yet *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* arises entirely from within space."
Then, how could there be what is called "dharma," and how could there be what is called "dharma" that can be spoken of?
Linzi said: "I create my own nature and destiny, and I return again to empty space;
since Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi emerges from this, it is said that there is not even the slightest dharma."
One may attain what is called one's own created nature, yet it returns to emptiness; this is why it is called "non-dharma.
As for the saying, "even dharma should be relinquished," it means to relinquish this very dharma. However, the meaning of the two characters "even" (乃至) must not be ignored:
it begins with having something attained; having attained something, one attains attainment, yet it is not a case of having something attained.
"Finally, there is nothing to be attained; yet by attaining through non-attainment, one attains that which is not non-attainment.
Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva said, "To reach the point where there are no words or letters is truly to enter the Dharma-gate of non-duality;
even the two characters 'Mañjuśrī' themselves carry this same meaning. From this, I realized that those who have not reached the other shore cannot [attain it].
If one has already reached the other shore, how can one still rely on the Dharma? An ancient said: "To cross a river one must use a raft;
once the shore is reached, the boat is no longer needed. If one cannot yet let go of the Dharma, it means one has not yet reached the shore.
How could there be anyone who has already reached the shore and yet remains mired in the raft? Therefore, one must surely reach the ultimate state.
When there is not even the slightest dharma to be apprehended and no words or letters,
only then can one be said to have truly reached the other shore, truly entered the gate of non-duality,
and truly attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Linzi said: "One should abide in this manner and subdue the mind in this manner;
this is precisely how one gives rise to the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*."
Linzi said: "What the Tathāgata calls 'all dharmas' are not what the world calls 'all dharmas.
Rather, they are produced by their own transformation and made empty; it is through this spontaneity that there is what is called 'all dharmas.
If one were to take what the world calls 'all dharmas' and call them 'all dharmas,' would that be appropriate? Therefore, it is said: 'It is precisely not one.'"
Because all dharmas are thus, they are called "all dharmas.
Master Linzi said: "How could there be wholesome dharmas within empty space? Is it not the case that while not a single dharma is established, all myriad dharmas are fully present?
Therefore, the Tathāgata says: "What is not a wholesome dharma is called a wholesome dharma."
Linzi said: "If one seeks me by means of form or pursues me through sound, this is because they do not know that the Tathāgata is the emptiness of self-nature.
Not knowing that the Tathāgata is the emptiness of self-nature, how could they not be called non-Buddhists?"
Subhūti said: "Does the Tathāgata attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* by virtue of possessing the marks of perfection?
Or does the Tathāgata attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* without possessing the marks of perfection?
If you hold that the Tathāgata attains *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* by virtue of possessing the marks of perfection..."

"Ti, if the Tathāgata also possesses all marks, he is not the Tathāgata. If you think that the Tathāgata attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* because he does not possess the marks of perfection, then the Tathāgata would also possess the mark of annihilation, and thus he would not be the Tathāgata.
Indeed, although all phenomena are present within empty space, in reality it is devoid of them."
Although all phenomena possess all characteristics, in reality they lack all characteristics.
Since there are no phenomena at all, how could there be any phenomena to be described?
Since there are no characteristics at all, how could there be any characteristics to be extinguished?
Linzi said: "The Tathāgata of the empty self-nature does not know of forms, much less of dharmas;
he does not know of dharmas, much less of teachings. Therefore, within the unmoving suchness there are no forms; yet within the unmoving suchness, though there are no forms, there are forms.
Within the unmoving suchness there are no dharmas; yet within the unmoving suchness, though there are no dharmas, there are dharmas. Suchness is unmoving.
Within movement there is no speaking; yet, within non-speaking, there is speaking. Linzi said:
"The Tathāgata is fundamentally empty space; therefore, his measure is equal to empty space. Linzi said:
"Where there is true empty space, there is a true world; and that which is called 'world' is not the mundane world."
Because it is the world of the realms, it is said: "It is not a world; it is called a world. Since there is true empty space, there is true Buddha-land;
yet what is called a Buddha-land is not a Buddha-land as a Buddha-land. Therefore, it is said: "It is not an adornment; it is called an adornment."
Linzi said: "If there were true emptiness, then there would be true *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
By what do you define your own *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*? That which you call *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* is, in fact, not *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*."
"Bodhi. The Forest Dweller said: "If there is true emptiness, then there is true prajñāpāramitā.
By what do you designate that as 'your' prajñāpāramitā? For that which you call prajñāpāramitā is precisely..."
"It is not the Prajñāpāramitā.
The forest-dweller said, "When the Buddha speaks of such profound sūtras, he refers to what is called the profound *dharmadhātu* and the *prajñā-samādhi*.
If it were not for the fact that one's own life-force is returned to the void, how could this exist?"
"Are there not these profound sūtras? Is there not this profound dharma-realm? Is there not this prajñā-samādhi? The Forest-Dweller replied:
"Does the Tathāgata have any dharma that he has taught? The Tathāgata has no dharma that he has taught. Long ago, Śākya...
As Kāśyapa was about to enter *nirvāṇa*, the Great Being Mañjuśrī requested the Buddha to turn the wheel of the Dharma once more. Śākyamuni rebuked him, saying:
"Mañjuśrī, during my forty-nine years of dwelling in the world, I have never spoken a single word.
Do you ask me to turn the wheel of the Dharma again because I have ever turned it before? Even at the assembly on Vulture Peak, that is now impossible to verify."

Regarding the various sutras he authored and discussed, one might ask: "Are these not teachings where the Wheel of Dharma was turned? Yet he says that not a single word was ever spoken—how can this be?
Whenever I have questioned eminent scholars on this matter, none have been able to explain the true meaning of Kāśyapa;
how much less so those of lesser caliber? Yet they claim that not a single word was spoken during the assembly on Vulture Peak—is this truly so?
"If it were not so, and yet all the twelve divisions of the sūtras spoken by the Buddhas were entirely useless in the world," Linzi said,
"the true meaning of Śākyamuni is likewise found only within the True Sūtras of the Tathāgata. Therefore,
by using my Tathāgata to interpret the Tathāgata of Śākyamuni, [one realizes] the truth of Śākyamuni."

The Sūtra is within me; since the True Sūtra is within me, why must I necessarily rely on what the ancients called the twelve divisions of the scriptures, and why should I worry that the ancient twelve divisions cannot be clearly understood?
Linzi asked, "What is it that you call the Vajra? He replied, "I do not know. Linzi said, "Your true sutra is your Vajra.
He asked, "What is it that you call the true sutra? He replied, "I do not know. Linzi said, "Your empty space is your true sutra.
He asked, "What is it that you call empty space? He replied, "I do not know. Linzi said:

This is not what the world calls "empty space. That you are able to know how to create your own nature and destiny while remaining empty—that is true emptiness. Only this emptiness is your true scripture;
it is your Vajra.
Master Linzi said: "That which takes the life and nature of one's parents as its own life and nature is the Tathāgata of the form body (rūpakāya).
That which makes the life and nature it has created of its own accord empty space is the Tathāgata of the dharma body (dharmakāya).
Therefore, the Tathāgata of the form body remains on this shore, while the Tathāgata of the dharma body has reached the other shore. Regarding the Tathāgata of the form body...
The Tathāgata of the form-body (rūpakāya) comes and thus obstructs the physical frame; the Tathāgata of the dharma-body (dharmakāya), however, encompasses the entire realm of space.
The Tathāgata of the form-body possesses intelligence but lacks true wisdom; the Tathāgata of the dharma-body possesses wisdom but has no need for mere intelligence.
Thus, the Tathāgata of the form-body belongs to the sphere of seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing, whereas the dharma-body does not.
The Tathāgata as such does not belong to seeing, hearing, sensing, or cognizing;
whereas the Tathāgata as the form-body (rūpakāya) possesses all mental characteristics, all dharma-characteristics, and all non-dharma characteristics.
The Tathāgata as the dharma-body (dharmakāya), however, possesses no mental characteristics, no dharma-characteristics, and no non-dharma characteristics—unlike the Tathāgata as the form-body.

The Dharmakāya Tathāgata regarding all phenomena as having the characteristic of cessation and extinction; the Rūpakāya Tathāgata regarding all phenomena as being without the characteristic of cessation and extinction;
the Dharmakāya Tathāgata regarding phenomena with a mind of grasping and rejecting;
the Rūpakāya Tathāgata regarding phenomena without a mind of grasping and rejecting; and the Dharmakāya [Tathāgata] regarding phenomena as having arising and ceasing...
The Tathāgata is such that, regarding the Dharma, there is neither arising nor ceasing; yet the physical body (rūpakāya) is also called the Tathāgata.
Master Linzi said: "I do not know from which scripture the 'Tathāgata of the physical body' is derived, yet the *Direct Explanation* of the Sixth Patriarch also contains this statement.
Is what he calls the 'Tathāgata of the physical body' not simply the consciousness-spirit (*vijñāna*)? Master Linzi replied: "No."
It is not so. All sentient beings, down to the most minute insects, possess Buddha-nature; this Buddha-nature is contained within the seeds of one's parents and is one's own spirit.
When the followers of Śākyamuni speak of "not valuing one's own spirit," they are referring precisely to this nature inherent in sentient beings.
From antiquity until now, the Buddhas have transmitted the Dharma to one another, none of whom have failed to rely upon this inherent nature.

If one follows the nature of the spirit to spontaneously engage in transformation, thereby re-establishing one's nature and destiny and returning to the void, only then can one behold the Tathāgata and realize unexcelled, perfect enlightenment. He asked again, "Is Buddha-nature not the Buddha?
Master Linzi replied, "It is not the Buddha. "If so, how is it able to become a Buddha? Master Linzi said, "Because it possesses [it]."
This is precisely what constitutes buddha-nature; therefore, one can become a Buddha. Do you alone not see how a sparrow becomes a clam?

The sparrow is a feathered insect that, by obtaining the vital energy (*qi*), uses its wings to soar through the air; the clam is a shelled insect that, by obtaining water, uses it to swim and wallow.
Is it not because their forms are dissimilar that this occurs? Yet, when one examines their nature and disposition, they are likewise [capable].
There are vast differences between things, yet it is known to all that a sparrow can transform into a clam;
have you not seen the *Monthly Ordinances* (*Yueling*) and the official calendars?

Do not say that the sparrow lacks consciousness—how could it otherwise undergo such a transformation into a clam? Little do you realize that this is obtained from Heaven, and there is what is called...
The true knowledge of sentient beings resides herein; it is the same for human beings as well. Therefore, it is said that this Buddha-nature exists.
It is acceptable to say that one relies upon the self-creation of one's own nature and destiny to transform and thereby achieve Buddhahood;
however, it is unacceptable to say that this Buddha-nature does not rely upon the self-creation of one's own nature and destiny to transform and thereby achieve Buddhahood.
Master Linzi said: "I have also compared this to the kernel within a fruit seed;
it is likewise a single point of seed-nature within the mother's womb. Containing and preserving the causal ground, it sprouts its bud;
from this, it develops branches, then leaves, then flowers, and finally fruits. Is this not what is meant by practicing according to the Dharma to realize [enlightenment]?"
If one merely contemplates stillness to empty the mind and claims that the Buddha-nature inherent in all sentient beings can achieve Buddhahood in the present moment, this is certainly not the case.
This is the fruit of Buddhahood of the Supreme One Vehicle.
Master Linzi said: "Whether born from an egg, born from a womb, born from moisture, or born by transformation; whether possessing form or being formless;
whether possessing perception, lacking perception, or neither possessing nor lacking perception—all possess Buddha-nature.

Since all possess Buddha-nature, all are capable of becoming Buddhas. Therefore it is said: 'A single thought-moment of turning back the mechanism [of delusion] is identical to attaining what was originally possessed.'"
However, why is this called "turning the mechanism"? Master Lin said:
"The transformation of the void becomes spirit; the transformation of spirit becomes qi; the transformation of qi becomes form.
When form returns to become qi, and qi returns to become spirit, and spirit returns to become the void—this is the turning of the mechanism."
Linzhi said: "To refer to the physical body as the Tathāgata, though it is not the true Tathāgata, is nonetheless permissible because it possesses this Buddha-nature and these sentient beings;
for when at times there is a wholesome thought, or when there is the mind to become a Buddha, one may also be called a Tathāgata. Yet, these wholesome thoughts and the mind to become a Buddha..."
"Is it appropriate or not to call that which is repeatedly seized and led away by emotional consciousness 'True Suchness' (Tathatā)?

It seems this depends entirely upon the interval between maintaining [the mind] or abandoning it; for when one masters mindfulness, and when one lacks it, the difference between the sage and the madman is vast.
Linzi said: "Do you mean that the nature of these sentient beings is the eternally constant nature, or is it not the eternally constant nature?"
Yet the Buddhas take this very nature as their own creative transformation (zàohuà) through which they perceive the Tathāgata.
Do you consider this nature of sentient beings to be the true, eternal nature, or is it not the true, eternal nature?

If the mind does not take this nature of sentient beings as its own creative transformation, it will be difficult indeed to attain Buddhahood and perceive the Tathāgata; nevertheless, when one investigates it to its ultimate limit, this is so.
They are nothing more than ghosts of a single *skandha*’s spirit.
Master Lin said: "All seed-natures (*gotra*) contain sentient beings, and all sentient beings possess Buddha-nature; therefore, the Buddha-nature within sentient beings is the seed of the Buddha.
Yet, one must rely upon this to fashion one's own destiny and nature, for [without it] it would be like empty space."
That which [realizes] this is the seed of the Buddha.
Linzi said: "If one speaks of the rectification of nature and destiny (*xingming*) in terms of the creative transformation of one's parents, it is called 'seed-nature' (*zhongxing*);
seed-nature, then, enters into birth and death. If one speaks of the rectification of nature and destiny in terms of the creative transformation of one's own body, it is called 'Dharma'."
The nature of dharmas does not enter into birth-and-death.
Master Linzi said: "Where there are the four great elements, there is the form of a body; where there is the form of a body, there is birth and death.
Yet now, having fashioned one's own destiny, one returns to the Great Void. How could there then be what is called 'birth' or what is called 'death'?"
"How extraordinary!
Master Linzi asked: 'Why is it said that by departing from the provisional, one realizes the true mind? [The Master replied:
'It is simply because, by departing from the provisional marks of this physical body, one returns to the real marks of my Dharma-body; there is nothing else to it.'"
Linzi said: "Why is it called practicing in accordance with the Dharma? To act as the creator for oneself is precisely to practice in accordance with the Dharma;
thus, the true mark (dharmatā) is inherently within me."
Linzi said: "Why is it called the essence of the pure mind, and why is it further said that 'one who has attained entry should abide thus and subdue thus'?
Is this not precisely the means by which one enters the essence of the pure mind? Therefore it is said:
'Upon hearing the instruction, one immediately attains awakening and entry; the original true nature spontaneously manifests.'"
Linzi said: "To establish all the gates of the teachings upon the true nature—does this not mean that one is creating things for oneself?"
Linzi said: "Why is it called the Reward Body Buddha? The self-nature manifesting of itself is precisely the Reward Body Buddha.
If one does not awaken to it oneself and cultivate it oneself, failing to see the self-nature, how could one be said to be able to take refuge in oneself?
Therefore, 'awakening' refers to awakening to the self-nature oneself; 'cultivation' refers to cultivating the self-nature oneself; and 'taking refuge' refers to taking refuge in oneself."
One takes refuge in one's own nature (*svabhāva*). Now, what is meant by "nature"? Nature is the original nature;

the original nature is the true nature (*dharmatā*). If one does not know how to cultivate one's own life and destiny, how could one possibly attain this true nature that has been inherently possessed from the beginning?
Linzi said: "The Buddha is fundamentally not a physical body; yet, within that which is not a physical body, one can perceive the Tathāgata of self-nature—this is truly seeing the Tathāgata.
Linzi said: "To take the life and nature of one's parents and treat them as one's own life and nature is to seek outwardly for a Buddha with form."
To take one's own created nature and destiny as the very nature and destiny [of reality] is to seek the formless Buddha within.

The *I Ching* says, "The Way of Qian undergoes transformation, and each rectifies its nature and destiny," yet the *Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment* states that all "rectify their nature and destiny through lustful desire.
If they are already rectified through lustful desire, why is it also called "rectifying"?
Is it not because the union of male and female is the meeting of the essence of Earth and Heaven, their mutual harmony?
If the union of male and female is considered not to be the norm, then might the harmony between Earth and Heaven also not be considered the norm?
Yet, in the end, one cannot avoid the presence of intermingling and confusion; it is from this that the nature of the mandate of Heaven first arises, and from this that Qi first arises.
If one examines the nature of substance, it is from this that clarity and turbidity, thickness and thinness are distinguished.
If, however, one does not know how to transcend the physical form through oneself and act as the creator of transformation to utterly eliminate this nature of substance (qi-zhì-xìng),
how could one ultimately return to the nature of destiny (tiān-mìng-xìng) and restore my own void?
Linzi said: "If one realizes sudden enlightenment into the non-arising [of phenomena], then one knows how to act as the creator of transformation for oneself.
Once one knows how to act as the creator of transformation for oneself, only then can one truly perceive this Tathāgata of the Dharma-body.

If, however, one does not know how to act as the creator of transformation for oneself, one will inevitably seek the Tathāgata within the physical body; such a person is what is called a 'man outside the gate.'"

This explains that even if one undergoes ascetic practices for kalpas as numerous as motes of dust, how could it be said that one would thereby realize unsurpassed perfect enlightenment and attain the vision of this Dharmakāya Tathāgata?
Master Linzi said: "One fashions one's own nature and life from within emptiness; thus, by means of my true Dharma, I obtain myself."
This is the true essence. If one does not know the True Dharma and yet claims to be able to know my true essence, they have not yet attained it.
The true essence is the nature of true permanence. This nature of true permanence is without birth and without death;

yet the Sixth Patriarch said that "in every single thing there is its own nature which contains birth and death. Is this not because the nature of true permanence is not something that is not all-pervasive?
This is why one cannot help but transform oneself and restore one’s nature and destiny, and restore it to emptiness.
To restore one’s nature and destiny and restore it to emptiness—if this is not called transforming oneself, what is it?
Is it not my own true, eternal nature? And as for this true, eternal nature, can it ever be said to contain or receive birth and death?
How could it be said that there is a place not reached before one may be named a Tathāgata?
Master Linzi said: "Reaching this stage is the Bodhimanda; it is the true ground of Nirvāṇa; it is neither defiled nor pure;
it is neither form nor emptiness; it is the forgetting of both person and phenomena; it is sinlessness."
Blessing has no master; this is the Great Way. It is vast and empty, which is the equality of nature and characteristics. It is the original nature, void and non-existent;
yet this voidness is a substantial reality. This is the eternally abiding true mind. To be sovereign according to the mind is the wondrous function of the Buddha.
To possess immeasurable bliss is for afflictions and karma to be purified. That which is originally empty and still is the cause of all things.
The fruits [of existence] are all like dreams and illusions; thus, the cessation of arising and ceasing is bliss.
The son of the Vṛji clan asked: "The Tathāgata is the Mother of Buddhas. Why, then, is the Tathāgata called the 'Mother'?"
Since all Buddhas are born from this, she is the Mother of Buddhas; "Mother of Buddhas" is the meaning of *tathatā* (suchness).

And because those who come from within that very *tathatā* are *Tathāgatas*, the Mother of Buddhas is fully endowed with the pure *dharmakāya*, yet the pure *dharmakāya* has never existed apart from the Mother of Buddhas. Thus, the Mother of Buddhas is fully endowed with...
The Buddha-Mother of the Perfect Dharmakāya has never been merely the Perfect Dharmakāya;
she is fully endowed with the thousands of billions of Nirmāṇakāyas, yet she has never been merely the thousands of billions of Nirmāṇakāyas—is she not indeed infinite?
From her proceed the Supreme Ultimate (Tàijí), the Two Polarities (Liángyí), and the Five Elements; yet the Buddha-Mother was never originally one of these. From her proceeds that One.
From two and three, all things are produced. Laozi called this "the Nameless," the beginning of heaven and earth;
Confucius called it "that which precedes heaven, which heaven does not oppose. Now we call it *xià* (the Primordial).
It is that state where there is as yet no Confucianism, no Daoism, and no Buddhism—merely *rú-rú* (suchness). It is from this that one names it.
Those who are Confucians, Daoists, or Buddhists are the *tathatā* (suchness).
Furthermore, that which is called "prior," before heaven existed, before earth existed, before the sun existed, and before the moon existed, is simply *tathatā*.
From this, the unfolding into heaven, earth, sun, and moon is the Tathāgata.
An appended response to the Confucian Linzi on "not abiding in signs":
Now, among the flourishing schools of the Confucians, none surpasses Zhongni (Confucius), yet even Zhongni was likewise so.

The *Daxue* says: "When the superior honors the aged, the people will be inspired to practice filial piety; when the superior honors the elderly, the people will be inspired to practice fraternal respect;
when the superior shows compassion for the orphaned, the people will not turn their backs on them.
The *Zhongyong* says: "Vastness and thickness are what sustain all things; loftiness and brilliance are what cover all things; eternity is what completes all things."

Furthermore, by practicing *dāna* (giving) without dwelling on signs, one brings about parinirvāṇa without remainder. By abiding in the ultimate good, the family is harmonized, the state is governed, and the world is brought to peace;
through the "centrality prior to arousal," one establishes the heavens and earth and nurtures the myriad things.
By practicing *dāna* without dwelling on signs, one brings about parinirvāṇa without remainder. And as for what is called "being manifest without being seen"—it is not...

As for how things move yet transform, and act without striving yet achieve completion—how could it be that only the people of the world do not know why they manifest, why they transform, and why they achieve completion? Even a sage would say:
"I have never seen anything, moved anything, or done anything; so how is it that I am able to manifest, transform, and achieve completion in this way? Therefore...
It is said that even all the great śrāvakas and up to the great bodhisattvas cannot fathom the Buddha’s wisdom; this is what is meant. Master Linzi said:

"As for the common people who beat the *rang* toy, what power does the Emperor have over them? This is the non-abiding in marks (*animitta*) of Yao of Tang. "He did nothing yet all was governed; he respectfully stood facing south.
This is the non-abiding in marks of Shun of Yu. "Wherever he established [the people], they were established; wherever he led them, they were led. This is the non-abiding in marks of the Way.
"Acting with gentleness, they come; moving them, they harmonize"—this was the non-abiding in marks (*animitta*) of Zhongni.

It is like manifesting form so it becomes visible, and making what is visible so it becomes clear; it is like moving and transforming until one undergoes spiritual change. It is also like exhausting the nature of humans and exhausting the nature of things, thereby participating in Heaven and Earth and assisting in the transformation and nourishment of all beings.
It is also like the people being respectful before respect has been bestowed, and [the Way] being practiced before it has been applied.
To be trusted so that the people trust him is like benefiting the people by following what they find advantageous—bestowing kindness without expense;

like laboring without resentment, or even dying without resentment at being killed; like the ultimate ritual being without ornate form yet sharing the same rhythm as Heaven and Earth, and the ultimate music being without sound yet sharing the same harmony as Heaven and Earth; it is also like striking a stone and clapping another stone together.

The hundred beasts led one another in dance as the *xiao* and *shao* music was performed nine times and the phoenixes came with graceful bearing; likewise, when the two steps were graced by the *qian-yu* dance, the Prince of Miao came to submit.
When the sage of the Middle Kingdom appeared, the seas did not toss their waves. Furthermore, all things possessing blood and breath—none failed to revere and love him;
even the spirits of the mountains and rivers found peace, and down to the birds, beasts, fish, and turtles, all were at ease.

It is as if the people are unable to name it or find anything by which to praise it; it is like the virtue that is not manifest, yet the various lords take it as their model and thereby reach the pinnacle of governance.
It is as if I wished to remain without words, yet there is nothing hidden from you—this constitutes the spiritual nature of teaching.

Furthermore, that those who knew him through sight and those who knew him through hearing, separated by more than five hundred years, were moved by a resonance across vast ages that cannot be artificially induced.

It is a matter of reflection. Furthermore, it is like knowing the principles of the Di sacrifice; when viewing the whole world from that perspective, the sacrificial rites are so profound and subtle that they cannot be grasped through mere conjecture.
Moreover, it is as if heaven and earth stand side by side with humanity to form the Three Powers (the *sancai*);

this does not mean merely that one’s mouth speaks on behalf of Heaven and one’s body acts on behalf of Heaven, but rather that the processes of creation and transformation (*zaohua*) are held within one’s own hands, and the primal mandate (*yuansheng*) is realized through oneself.
Once the work is done, it is turned and completed; its subtle efficacy is so minute as to be unfathomable.
As for what is called "giving without dwelling on signs" (animitta-dāna), whereby all things are extinguished without remainder—is this not true not only of the Śākya school?
The Great Body Forest Master said: "It is because of Da (the Dao) that Yao and Shun were able to exist;
thus, the Great Harmony and Primordial Qi can circulate within the universe. Precisely because this Great Harmony and Primordial Qi can circulate within the universe," [the universe...]
Is all within the universe not the one great body of Yao and Shun?
Even when reduced to the state of Zhongni [Confucius], his vast and righteous qi (*haoran zhengqi*) was nonetheless able to fill the space between heaven and earth.
Since it is precisely because this vast and righteous qi can fill the space between heaven and earth, the space between heaven and earth is nothing other than the one great body of Zhongni.

Yet this [body] still exists within the universe and between heaven and earth; how much more so, then, regarding that which is called the "substance of emptiness" (*ākāśa-svabhāva*)—that is, the "emptiness as the fundamental substance" (*svabhāva-ākāśa*)?
This is precisely what the Confucians mean by the "Great Vacuity of the same substance.
Therefore, it is said that that which is not a body is called the "Great Body."
The *Yījīng* says: "Change and movement do not abide; they circulate through the six voids. Furthermore, the *Lúnyǔ* says: "The higher one looks up at it, the higher it rises;
the harder one drills into it, the harder it becomes. Looking for it, it seems to be in front; suddenly, it is behind.

Is this not because the Way is fundamentally empty and void—having neither high nor low, neither interior nor exterior, neither far nor near—and its measure is simply the suchness of the direct nature?
Thus, it is inherently as vast as this: yet, since nature is the Way and the Way is benevolence (*ren*), heaven, earth, and the myriad things are all encompassed within my Tathāgata’s Dharma-body.
Master Cheng said: "For the benevolent person, heaven, earth, and the myriad things constitute a single body;
the *ren* of the Confucian school is the Tathāgata of the Buddhist school. Therefore, it is said that one is able [to realize this].
"Benevolence" (*ren*) is [the teaching of] Śākyamuni, yet the Śākya clan is also called "benevolent. Zengzi said: "To take benevolence as one's own responsibility—is it not heavy?
If one bears such a heavy responsibility, how could they not be called 'one who carries the Tathāgata on their shoulders'?
When all things are fully present and one turns back to realize sincerity, first establishing that which is great—this is what is meant by a "Great Man" (*mahāpuruṣa*).
Wushuo said,
"Master Gongzi remarked that the nature of humanity and the Way of Heaven are things one cannot hope to hear.
Judging now by what Gongzi has said, how could it be that what is called 'nature' and the 'Way of Heaven' can actually be spoken of?"
"Is there anything that can be heard? Therefore it was said: "I wish to remain without words," for the means by which he taught were ultimate.
Ziguang did not realize this and asked, "If you do not speak, how shall we, your disciples, transmit [your teachings]?
Now, if even speaking cannot be spoken, how much less can it be heard? And if hearing cannot be heard, then...
How much less can it be fully described? Confucius said, "I have nothing hidden from you.

Does this not mean that within the state of no-words there naturally exists the ultimate word? Therefore, those who do not understand the Way take the Way to be hidden in no-words, while those who do understand the Way take the Way to be hidden in words.
Regarding the fruit of Buddhahood and the fruit of Arhatship, Master Lin said: "To cross over oneself but not to cross over others is the fruit of Arhatship.
One who first seeks to cross over others before crossing over themselves possesses a great vow; though it is said they can deliver all people in the world, their heart..."
Yet they still consider that the fruit of Buddhahood has not been reached; how could it be only for those of the Śākya clan?
That which is called "the aged being at peace, friends being trusted, and the young being cherished" is the fruit of Buddhahood of Confucius.

To be virtuous without boasting of it, to labor without seeking reward, and to share one's carriage, horse, light robe, and fur cloak until worn out without regret—this was the Arhat-fruit of Yan Hui and Ji Lu.

Yu the Great thought of those drowning in the world as if he himself were drowning them; Houji thought of those starving in the world as if he himself were starving them—this is the fruit of Buddhahood (*buddhatva*).
Had it been their time, would Nao Fu and Xu You not have said that the pure breeze was sufficient to refresh all people?
Yet those who cultivate only their own persons to be lofty and pure achieve only the fruit of an Arhat (*arhattva*).
The Forest-Dweller of the Tathāgata said: "There is no thought and there is no action; it is tranquil and unmoving, yet it penetrates all under heaven as soon as it is stimulated."
Therefore, the "Ancient" is the Tathāgata. What need is there for the world to think or deliberate? The world returns to the same goal by different paths;

though there are a hundred deliberations, they accord with one principle—this is the Tathāgata. What does Heaven say? Yet the four seasons proceed and the hundred things are born—this is the Tathāgata.
Vast and profound, like a spring from which all issues forth at the proper time—this is the Tathāgata. Sincerity is the Way of Heaven.

The Tathāgata is one who attains realization without deliberation and hits the mark without exertion; the Tathāgata is one whose "central state" (zhong) is soundless and odorless yet unmanifested, such that all its manifestations accord with the proper measure;
the Tathāgata is one who observes the soaring of the falcon and the leaping of the fish to discern the upper and lower realms;
the Tathāgata is one who, upon suddenly seeing a child fall into a well, possesses a heart of alarm, distress, and compassion.
Therefore, that which takes utility as its root and issues forth in accordance with it is the Tathāgata.
That which possesses innate knowledge such that it knows without deliberation and possesses innate capacity such that it acts without deliberation is the Tathāgata.

That which is like a spring gushing forth, flowing unceasingly day and night, is the Tathāgata. To dwell securely, to draw from a profound source, and to encounter the fountainhead at every turn—this is the Tathāgata.
The Tathāgata is simply the essence of constant clarity and constant awakening, vast and universally impartial; yet it is the Tathāgata who responds in accordance with the arrival of things.

It is the Tathāgata whose single point of numinous light is vividly bright and never obscured, such that the loyalty of a loyal minister and the filiality of a filial son surge forth irresistibly. Thus, the Tathāgata is none other than myself.
The Dharma-body of the Tathāgata fills the Dharma-realm. To speak of its greatness, nothing in the world can contain it;
to speak of its smallness, nothing in the world can break it. Thus it is said that "all things are complete within me," and this is precisely how the Sage unifies the whole world as a single body.
Nevertheless, heaven and earth are likewise but one thing within my Way.
If I attain centrality through myself and attain harmony through myself—once centered and harmonized—would Heaven and Earth not find their proper place through me?
Therefore, if I practice the learning of the Confucian school, my own person is itself a Confucius;
how could I not be Confucius? And if I practice the learning of the Daoist school, my own person is itself...
"This is the Elder (Laozi), yet am I not that Elder? If I take myself to be the study of the Śākya clan, then my own person is itself a Śākyamuni; yet am I not that Śākyamuni?
However, as for the Tathāgata within my own person, is there any difference between him and the Śākyamuni, the Elder, and Confucius? He replied: "There is no difference."
Furthermore, how could one know that what penetrates within heaven and earth and what penetrates beyond heaven and earth are all my very self?

They are all my very self; they are all the Tathāgata. Therefore, to take this "self" and abide in the Mean (*zhong*) to establish the foundation for teaching is precisely my Tathāgata, Confucius. To take this "self" and abide in purity and stillness...
To enter the gate and take this as the teaching is my Tathāgata, who is also Laozi;
to abide in me in tranquil concentration and reach the ultimate limit and take this as the teaching is my Tathāgata, who is Śākyamuni.
The five chapters above are all the words of the Confucian school;

yet when one compares them with what the followers of Śākyamuni call the "inconceivable" and the "immeasurable," if one were able to view them side by side, the words of the Buddhists would all be found to be truthful.
However, because [the Confucians] have not yet reached such a state, they cannot avoid being startled and filled with doubt.

This is a slanderous claim. The *Analects* states that the Master rarely spoke of destiny (*ming*) and benevolence (*ren*), and that [the nature of man] and the Way of Heaven (*tian dao*) were things even Zi Gong—despite his brilliant insight—could not hope to hear about, let alone others.
Therefore, these responses to questions have been appended to the end of the manuscript. By Lin Zimiao.
